How this is worked out: how this page stays current

The page is rebuilt from live mWater every Monday morning, and on demand in between. Every figure on it comes from a named population, a cited parameter or a dated manual file, and opens to show how it is produced when you click it. A build that fails any of its checks is not published, so the page you are reading is always the last one that passed every check; the dates above say when it was issued and how fresh its data is.

SaniTap Water Portfolio

One page for the whole safe-water portfolio: MadAvance hand pumps (live from mWater) and Endur'O piped systems (manual figures until Endur'O is on mWater). Built for programme managers: running the work, keeping the Gold Standard file clean, and reporting to donors.

Scope

How this is worked out: what the portfolio is

The portfolio is the water points we actively manage: pumps we maintain and that serve people, broken ones included. A broken pump stays in the portfolio and is counted as down until it is repaired.

Records that only sit in the MadAvance mWater group — survey and identification entries, abandoned points, points handed on to others, other pump types — are not part of the portfolio and are not counted anywhere on this page.

Endur’O’s piped systems are included on the figures Endur’O supplies by hand, dated, until they are on mWater. Marolinta’s pumps are in the managed portfolio because we have taken them on as they are built, although none has had a preventive visit or repair yet; they are funded separately and sit outside the carbon programme: they appear in no carbon figure.

Business as usual goes live. Provisional until Adriaan or Jan approves: (a) an existing record edited so that credits or eligibility go up; (b) a record deleted; (c) a large week-on-week move in carbon credits, points in scope or people served carried by edited records. Abandoned, removed or non-functional pumps with a supporting record pass without approval. A repository edit that moves a headline figure carries a decision in data/decisions.json naming who instructed it (rule of 7 Oct 2026).

How this is worked out: how a pump joins or leaves

Every run, the build reads the whole MadAvance register in mWater. A record joins the portfolio on its own when it has all four of: a successful first rehabilitation, a district that is one of our sites, a GPS position, and a recognised pump model (Canzee, IndiaMark). A record the build cannot place is held back for review: it goes to the build log and does not appear on this page. A pump leaves only by a recorded decision, with its evidence, listed under the register corrections. Every change to membership is dated.

How this is worked out: water quality per pump

For each pump, the latest result on the SDWS 3 water-quality results form, recalculated from mWater on every run. A result passes when E. coli is at or below 0 CFU per 100 mL; any higher count fails. A pump with no result is shown as not tested, never as passed.

How this is worked out: how people served is counted

“People served” is allocated, not tested. It is the population the model allocates to the water points, plus Endur’O’s agreed figure where the scope includes it. It is not a count of people whose water has passed a test; that is the E. coli chart, pump by pump. A higher figure under the proposed India Mark cap, awaiting James Walker, is shown beside it there and in the partner table; the page uses today’s cap until he confirms.

Population, not a headcount. The population comes from WorldPop R2025A v1, 2025, constrained, 100 m (file checksum 838c2fc72e49…). Each pump is given the people living within 1,000 m of it. People on the far side of an insurmountable barrier — a river with no bridge or ford, or the coast — are left out, as the methodology requires; the barrier lines are drawn past the edge of the circle before it is cut, so a river that crosses the circle always divides it, and only the part holding the pump is kept. Where the areas of two or more pumps overlap, the people in the overlap are split equally between them, so nobody is counted twice. Each pump is then capped at what it can physically deliver: 500 people for a Canzee, 300 for an India Mark. The cap is our own conservative safeguard, not a requirement of the methodology.

People per pump is that figure divided by the maintained pumps in each district; Marolinta is left out.

When a pump joins or leaves, the allocation is rerun for that pump and every pump within 2,000 m of it, because their shares of the overlap change. Nothing further away may move; if anything does, the build stops and nothing is published.

The roof count is a cross-check only, not the figure of record: the roofs recorded around each pump, divided by 2.5 roofs per household, times 4.5 people per household (the registered ex-ante value for Anosy, used for this cross-check everywhere; the external people-per-premises source for monitoring, the INSTAT census, is discussed with people per premises).

30 Sep 2026: barrier split fixed; a rounding error had left some river crossings uncut since 16 Sep; the figure before and after is 128,634 → 125,710 people served (after the pump caps, all managed pumps). The rules did not change. The river lines were cut off exactly at the edge of each 1,000 m circle, their ends missed the edge by a rounding margin, and the circle was then often left whole: points losing more than a tenth of their service area were 122 and are now 366. The pipeline, sdws1_population.py, now draws the lines past the edge and checks that the pieces make up the whole circle; its sha256 is in the provenance below.

The fleet at a glance

Hand pumps only (live). Status is the last thing anyone recorded about each pump, in any year — a call-centre contact, a preventive-maintenance visit or a repair. The date of that record is shown with it, and some are older than 2026.

How a pump’s status is decided. Status is the last thing anyone recorded about a pump. A call-centre contact, a preventive-maintenance visit and a repair each carry their own question, and each answer maps to working, partially working or not working; a record that never reached its question is skipped. The latest record by date wins, and on the same date the call wins. A pump with no answered record of any kind is unknown. Rebuilt every edition by tools/build_call_tables.py, which reproduces the published tables exactly from the extract they were built on (the cut of 2026-09-07) once the 39 pumps its rule cannot reproduce are held on their published value rather than restated on a guess, listed with a reason in data/call_status_holds.json; most are days on which a call and a visit share the last date and the extract gives no way to say which the original build followed. The split of “partially working” into a service request and a reduced-performance report could not be recovered either, so it is carried forward and new entries are left unclassified.

How status, “partially working” and the visit clock are defined

Working includes pumps whose guardian described them to the call centre as "partially working". That label is not used as a status: in most cases the guardian is requesting the routine service visit (the pump delivers water and is due for scheduled maintenance), and the remainder are reduced-performance reports (mechanical, low yield, water quality) which are tracked separately below for management follow-up. Unknown (“No status record”) = no answered call, visit or repair record in any year, or a pump held on its published “unknown” while the rebuilt rule disagrees (see the note below the charts). Time since last visit counts from the most recent preventive visit or repair, or — where there has been neither — from the date the pump was rehabilitated or constructed, so a pump commissioned last month is not counted as overdue. Pumps with no works record of any kind sit in their own bucket and are excluded from the overdue count until they are commissioned in mWater.

Management notes — internal, remove before sharing with a validation and verification body (VVB)

1. Call-centre wording. The call form offers guardians a small option list plus a free-text box. Most of them log a request for the routine six-monthly service visit using the word they were trained to use for the post-repair cleaning procedure, and a smaller group write maintenance préventive. Both mean the same thing: please send the scheduled service visit. Read literally by an outsider, the first wording implies the water is unsafe — it is not; these pumps carry passed E. coli tests. It is a training artefact of the call form, not a water-quality signal. The form fix and the retraining are on the action list. The table above now renders a normalised status derived from what the guardian wrote. The original free text is untouched in mWater and is one click away from every row via the mWater column, so nothing is hidden from a verifier — the record is the record. The fix is the form, not the history.

2. Field productivity. Median 3 pumps per field day, all teams together (preventive-maintenance records since Sep 2025), is low for pumps a few km apart. One likely driver is the per-diem system, which pays per field day and so rewards slow coverage over completed pumps. The redesign is on the action list.

Every asset on one map, one marker per pump, positions and photographs read live from mWater — the same record a verifier would open. Every MadAvance hand pump the register holds, and the Endur’O register now that it is readable.

What is on it, and what is not. Every MadAvance hand pump in the maintained register, with its field photographs, the sampled taps on the Moramanga axis, and the water points in Endur'O’s own mWater register. Those are not Endur'O’s southern programme sites, which come from the three-way reconciliation, are mostly not in mWater and are not in the managed portfolio (see the Endur’O card and the Endur'O estate section below). Antananarivo kiosks join the managed portfolio one at a time as they are onboarded — 1 so far, reported in the piped water-quality section and not drawn on this map; the Antananarivo sites not yet onboarded are diagnosed but outside the managed portfolio, and belong to the project pipeline. The southern UNICEF sites are likewise out of scope for this map. Hand-pump markers are drawn from mWater positions at the moment the page loads, so they cannot drift from the register.

Tell field teams: photograph the old calendar before replacing it act-calendar-custodyStanding rule, to be issued to every field team today: no calendar may be replaced until the previous one has been photographed and the photograph confirmed legible and uploaded. When a 2027 sheet is issued, the 2026 sheet stays at the water point. It is not removed, not taken away and not discarded. Sheets are replaced on a rolling basis — the SOP says so: “Les calendriers déjà posés sur le terrain restent au modèle 2024/2025 ; ils sont remplacés au fur et à mesure, sans campagne dédiée” — and a sheet that is gone cannot be re-photographed at any price. This rule was previously argued from a claim that 2027-dated sheets were being distributed nine months early. That claim was tested and does not hold — those sheets are in active use, not future stock. The rule stands on replacement happening at all, which it does. This is the precondition for the recovery round below — that round has nothing to photograph if the sheets have been thrown away first. The rule is written into SOP-MAD-SDWS27-CalendrierGardien as chapter 6 bis, added at v1.2 and carried forward unchanged into v1.3. What remains is issuing it to the teams, which is the part that protects sheets. The rule is deliberately stricter than “photograph it first”: the photograph must be confirmed legible and uploaded, because an illegible photograph of a discarded sheet is the same as no photograph.

Stays open (Adriaan Mol, 26 Sep 2026). The rule is confirmed unchanged in calendar SOP v1.7, chapter 6 bis.

Source: Adriaan Mol, COO SaniTap, “instruction for the water report”, 2026-09-26: Stays open.

Add Malagasy as a language on the preventive maintenance form act-mwater-mg-localeAdd the Malagasy locale to the Entretien préventif form, so Malagasy labels stop having to lead the French string. The form declares en and fr only. Every technician using it works in Malagasy, so Malagasy wording is currently smuggled into the French field — 2.15.7 reads “Taona voarakitra amin’ity teti-andro ity … / Année documentée par ce calendrier …” in one string, because there is nowhere else to put it. That is a workaround, and it degrades both languages: the French reads as an afterthought and the Malagasy cannot be shown on its own. Add mg to design.locales, then restore 2.15.7’s label and hint to their proper per-language fields. The other strings do not have to be translated in the same pass — mWater falls back to the base locale for any string without an mg value — but adding the locale is what makes translating them possible at all. The PoU form has the same gap.

Ask Gold Standard whether a stroke counter counts as a pump sensor act-sensor-definitionPut the sensor definition to Gold Standard. Ask whether a stroke counter constitutes an “operation sensor” for SDWS 27 (v1.0) / SDWS 32 (v2.0). Neither version defines the term — there is no definitions entry in either, and the phrase “monitoring device” appears nowhere in either document. But both versions connect the term to stroke counting in terms. v1.0 SDWS 23 Option 2: “Operation sensor measures directly operation time or pump stroke count”. And v2.0 SDWS 28 names them outright in its instrument row: “Operation sensors (e.g., stroke counters)”. So the residual question is narrower than it looked. v2.0 all but answers it; what is not written down is whether the same reading carries to the days-operational parameter — SDWS 27 in v1.0, which governs this crediting period and gives no such example — where the box says only “operation sensor”. This is the sole route to a days-operational figure above 347, on either version; if the answer is no, 347 is the ceiling for the life of the crediting period whatever the calendars show. Ask in the same letter as the SDWS 27 basis questions.

Template: SOP-MAD-SDWS27-CalendrierGardien-Template-v1.4-2027.pdf; procedure: SOP-MAD-SDWS27-CalendrierGardien-v1.7-2026. Print from the controlled generator SOP-MAD-SDWS27-CalendrierGardien-Generator-v1.4.py only — never from a working copy — and file the run against Template-v1.4. v1.4 stock carries no printed year: the period is written on the sheet when it is hung, beside the pump number, so a sheet can no longer assert a period it does not cover, and the same blank stock goes to any district without pre-assignment to a point. The grid is still laid out for a year — true month lengths and weekday letters — so a run is per year: pass --year to the generator and print 2026 and 2027 runs as needed. That is one variant per year, not 732, and it is what keeps the seventh impossible cell and the gardien’s weekday letter. Sequence it so no point is ever left without a sheet. Year-printed stock is withdrawn from a district only once v1.3 has physically arrived there; until then the old stock keeps being issued, because a point with no calendar produces no evidence at all. Sheets already hanging are not swapped out for this — they are replaced on the normal rolling basis and only after the custody rule above has been satisfied, the previous sheet photographed and the photograph confirmed legible and uploaded. Withdrawn year-printed stock is not reissued elsewhere. Where a v1.4 sheet is hung on a point whose old sheet is still being carried, the technician writes the year on both.

Find out what the year printed on calendars is meant to mean act-printed-year-meaningEstablish what the year printed on a gardien calendar is meant to denote, and whether sheets are issued with a forward year deliberately. This is the key the whole days-operational evidence chain turns on. Coverage, the observable window, the locking of cells on the transcription page and the year-by-year emission-reduction attribution all derive from the printed year. It has been shown not to denote the period the sheet records: sheets printed 2027 were photographed during 2026 with the months already elapsed at the photograph marked far more often than the months after — they are in service, not held in stock. The analysis that measured this is not in this repository, so its counts and rates are not restated here. Two questions for the print run and the field: is the printed year the edition or print run of the sheet, or the period it is intended to cover; and are sheets with a forward year issued deliberately — a batch printed ahead and put straight into use — or by mistake. Template v1.4 removes our dependence on the answer; it does not supply it. New stock prints no year at all and the technician writes the period on the sheet, so from the January round forward the question stops mattering for new evidence. It still matters for the sheets already in the field, which is every sheet the retrospective years rest on, and only the print run and the field teams can say whether a forward year was deliberate. Consequence if the answer is “edition, not period”: the reader must key on something other than the printed year, and the published coverage figures move — bounded and small, water points with 2026 evidence going from 299 to 308 on the 2026-dated-sheet basis. That technical change follows from the answer and is not raised as a separate action until there is one. Best asked in the same conversation as the undatable-sheet list above.

Define what approving an mWater record means, and use it sparingly act-mwater-approval-policyDefine what approving an mWater record means, then apply it only where it buys something. Neither methodology version requires record approval. It is our own workflow, and that matters: a bulk approval by someone who has not read the records is worse than none, because it manufactures assurance a verifier may then rely on. The previous version of this item asked for a different, larger number of records to be approved. That count is withdrawn: it was carried forward from a superseded basis. That was the wrong ask.

What is worth doing: a documented quality check, against stated criteria, on a sample of the 1,464 unapproved old-combined-works records. Those carry the SDWS 2 eligibility evidence for the portfolio and they are a finite historical set — the form has taken one submission all year — so a sample can speak for the whole of it, and the criteria can be written down once.

Explicitly out of scope. Blanket approval of the ongoing weekly forms: approving records as they arrive adds a signature and no scrutiny, and it would have to be done for ever. The call-centre form (2,820 unapproved): a dispatch record carries no carbon quantity, decided 21 September 2026, so approving one asserts nothing about anything this page reports.

Owner is the work, not the database. Approving a works record is a judgement about whether the work was done and evidenced, which is Angelo’s and Jan’s to make. It is not an administrative right, and it should not sit with the mWater group administrator.

Update the stroke-test procedure to the new methodology's condition act-v2-stroke-testReconcile the stroke-test SOP with v2.0, which recognises it and adds a condition. v1.0 SDWS 23 offers a flow meter or an operation sensor and nothing else. v2.0 SDWS 28 Option 3 adds: “Alternative Methods (Handpumps only): If Options 1/2 are infeasible/inappropriate/prohibited, recognized methods/proxies (e.g., standardised stroke tests) are permitted. Requires robust justification and VVB validation. Measurement may be on a sampling basis.” This settles the numbering question standing in our own SOP — under v2.0 the stroke test is SDWS 28 Option 3, not SDWS 27 Option 3. The quarterly validation in that box does not reach us. It reads “For Option 3, the developer shall validate the proxy against a direct measurement (Option 1 or 2) quarterly” — expressly scoped to Option 3, and Option 2 is one of the direct measurements Option 3 is validated against. The frequency row confirms it: “Continuously (Options 1 & 2) or Periodically (Option 3/Sampling)”. The StrokeMeter logger is an Option 2 sensor, so the plan’s annual re-verification of the fleet conversion factor stands unchanged. The reconciliation is done in the stroke-test SOP v2.2 drafts (French and English): SDWS 28 Option 3 throughout, 50 pump calibrations a year, annual re-verification, and the five-minute test as the standardised test. Bring preventive maintenance visits back to the planned rate (SDWS 27) act-restore-preventive-maintenance-visitRestore the preventive-maintenance visit rate (SDWS 27). The calendar practice never lapsed: 758 of the 761 preventive-maintenance visits on record carry a calendar photograph, 720 of them on 2.15.6, the field of record. Calendar currency is therefore a function of how often a point is visited, not of whether the procedure is followed. Visits have collapsed: 100 in March 2026, 45 in July, 10 in August. Fort-Dauphin has had no preventive-maintenance visit since June 2026, and none in October or November 2025. The 62 points with no calendar photograph and the 385 stale beyond six months are the arithmetic consequence of that, not a field-discipline failure. Consequence: the SDWS 27 evidence base degrades as the visit rate falls. The value applied is 347 days, the default for a project without operation sensors, and the calendars are the operation and maintenance log that evidences it. Track how fast the call centre sends technicians and reports back act-repair-timeCall-centre response and report-back time — an operational performance target, explicitly not a carbon figure. This is a dispatch metric. The call centre exists to send a technician to a pump; the gardien calendar is the official record of days operational, decided 21 September 2026. Nothing in this item feeds a carbon calculation. Baseline, 21 September 2026. Recorded repairs then ran at a median of 1 day and a p90 of 16 days from notification to completion, across 187 repairs on 145 points; today the median is 1 day and the p90 12 days across 192 repairs. That is not the whole picture and cannot be: the repair form is created only once the work is finished — 143 of 187 records carried a completion date equal to the submission date — so the system cannot represent outstanding work at all. Counted from the call centre instead, 44 tickets were open with no repair recorded since, at a median 84 days, p90 193, longest 258; 21 had been open more than three months. Fort-Dauphin held 64% of that backlog on 17% of the points. Three things are asked for. (1) Clear the 44, oldest first, Fort-Dauphin first given the concentration — and note that clearing a ticket may mean recording a repair that already happened, not doing one. (2) A target on two intervals that are not currently measured at all: report to technician dispatch, and dispatch to report-back. The existing median of 1 day measures neither — it measures repairs that were completed and recorded, entered from memory at the moment of completion. Set the target on p90 rather than the median, because the median is already 1 day and the tail is where the time goes. (3) A way to represent a repair in progress, which the present form cannot do. Until that exists, an open ticket and an unreported repair are indistinguishable, which is the reason the 44 cannot be read as downtime. Merged, not duplicated: this item began as a repair-time target and now carries the call-centre response and report-back scope as well, under the same owner and deadline. It also carries the SOP amendment recording that the 95% pause rule is not applied. A dependency runs the other way too: whether those 44 tickets are stale or the calendars are under-marked is settled by the transcription round, not by this item.

Closes when manual — Adriaan marks it done: Adriaan marks the call-centre response target set.

Photograph every surviving 2026 breakdown calendar at every pump act-2026-recoveryRun the 2026 calendar recovery round across the whole portfolio — not a sample. Photograph every surviving 2026 gardien calendar so 2026 becomes full-year evidence instead of partial. The denominator is all 732 carbon points — the actively managed register less Marolinta, computed every build, and coverage achieved is to be reported against that denominator and no other. Prioritise the 435 points with no dated 2026 sheet at all. The same round verifies that a calendar is physically present and legible at every point, which is a separate finding from whether it has been photographed — a point with no sheet on the wall needs a reissue, not a photograph. The round records the period at source, so attribution never depends on reading a printed header. Two steps, both before the shutter. First, the technician writes the year the sheet documents into the header, in pen — into the TAONA / ANNÉE box on v1.3 stock, or beside the pump identifier box on an older sheet — so the photograph itself carries the period. Second, the same year is entered as a field beside the photograph: a new whole-number question 2.15.7, “Année documentée par ce calendrier”, on the preventive-maintenance form de26d89a5c8a4452b42158c622be20d0, in question group d5233b2b immediately after 2.15.6, required whenever 2.15.6 carries an image. Where the year cannot be established from the sheet or from the gardien, the field is left empty and the period is treated as unproven — it is never filled in with the most likely year. Both steps are chapter 7 ter of the SOP. From the January round onward the period a sheet documents is recorded by the technician holding it, and is not inferred from the printed header. The question is live on the form as of 20 September 2026, id 3393e25651c047d0b8a29f34cdcf12d9, and is optional — stock already in the field carries no handwritten year, and a required field would force an invented answer. Making it required is a separate action below. The form carries French and English only, so the Malagasy wording — “Taona voarakitra amin’ity teti-andro ity” — leads the French label, as it does on the sheet itself; that too has its own action. Whole-portfolio, because the sampling question above is unsettled and the text leans against sampling the log; a sample would have to be redone if the answer is every point. Of 732 carbon points, 435 have no dated 2026 sheet at all. The tonnage and cash size of that gap is withdrawn with the per-year carbon basis it was computed from (act-carbon-year-basis) — the gap is those points, and it is evidence, not uplift: it protects the registered figure rather than exceeding it. A full-year 2026 record cannot be taken before 31 December 2026, by definition, so the round runs in January 2027. Field teams must be told immediately to leave the old sheet at the point when a new one is issued, and not to discard it. Replacement is rolling and continuous, so the evidence is at risk continuously rather than at a season. Feasibility is evidenced: sheets persist at points long after their year ends — 2024 sheets were still being photographed on 3 September 2026, twenty-one months later. Combine with the reissue round and the overdue preventive-maintenance round; the calendar is not a reason for a separate journey.

Record piped-system maintenance, repairs and downtime in mWater (SDWS 27) act-enduro-onboard-7-piped-sdws27Endur’O onboarding: piped maintenance, repair and days-not-operational records in mWater — the SDWS 27 evidence. Thirteen Piped Water forms exist — diagnostic, water point identification, kiosk installation and management, delivery and contact, construction/rehabilitation, baseline, and SDWS 3 sampling and results — but there is no piped equivalent of preventive maintenance, of repair-after-breakdown, or of days-not-operational. 3 of the three record types have no final record on a managed piped system in mWater. Days operational on the piped systems and kiosks is assessed per system, not per tap: outlets of the same system within 1 km of one another form one service unit (each Antananarivo kiosk is its own system), and on metered sites the metered volume is expected to be the binding term in Qy = min(Qm, Qpop). The sides are bare earth with roots and vegetation growing down into the water; two loose planks and a cut branch lie across part of the mouth. A black HDPE pipe runs to it in two of the three photographs, which suggests it is being drawn from — so people may be drinking from it now. The only record that does reference it is an unsubmitted draft on the borehole progress form, started 26 June 2026. Keep broken pumps in the register; never retire them for inactivity act-decommission-inactivity-fieldDecided 21 September 2026: SaniTap will not decommission or retire water points for inactivity. A pump that stays broken is a repair problem, not a register problem. It remains in the portfolio and is reported at its honest days operational. The reasoning is conservatism: removing under-performing points takes them out of the denominator and flatters the fleet average — the worst points leave the register and the reported availability of what remains rises, without a single pump working better. That is the less conservative treatment and the one a verifier would question. It is also what the methodology already assumes: neither version has any provision for a retired supply, because DOp,y is days operational and a pump that stops working simply contributes fewer of them. What follows: the 95% pause rule in the French suppression SOP is not applied and that SOP should be amended to say so; the permanent-deletion criteria are untouched, none of them being an availability judgement; no writable status property is needed in the register, because the only thing it was wanted for was a “paused” state that no longer exists, and the ZZ TEST name convention already handles the two records that are not water points; and repair speed becomes the only lever on days operational, which is why time to repair is now a headline metric above. Decision record, with the analysis that led to it: docs/decommissioning_rule_question.md. The original finding stands — the “jours d’inactivité” field exists on no live form — and is now moot for retirement, though the SOP amendment is not. Neither SOP is obsolete. Both carry permanent-deletion criteria that have nothing to do with availability — duplicate records, confirmed persistent contamination, irreparable or abandoned infrastructure, serious health or safety risk, a point taken over by another funder, no access — and all of those remain live. What is superseded is the 95% pause rule in the French SOP alone, which the English one never carried. That one clause should be struck; the documents stay.

Agree with Gold Standard how pump working days are evidenced (SDWS 27) act-sdws27-basisSettle the SDWS 27 basis with Gold Standard. Five questions, in one place, because they resolve together. (1) May the operation-and-maintenance log be demonstrated on a sample, or must it cover every water point? No sentence in either methodology version, or in the VPA-DD, settles this. But the text leans one way: the VPA-DD’s own sampling plan lists every parameter it intends to sample and SDWS 27 is absent; the sampling section is invoked from eight other parameter boxes in v1.0 and fifteen in v2.0 and from neither days-operational box; and the one express permission to sample anything under SDWS 27 attaches to the sensor route alone — “Operational sensors may be applied on a (90/10) sample basis”. We are planning on every point. (2) What happens to a point whose calendar is lost or illegible? Both documents are silent. “Illegible” and “missing” appear zero times in either; the four occurrences of “lost” in v2.0 are all “lost co-benefits” in the leakage sections. Exclusion, fallback to the registered estimate, or something else — there is no provision to quote. Our own SOP fills the gap with a conservative fallback, but that is a house rule no verifier is bound by, and it decides the treatment of 435 points. Then the three already open: (a) Is DOp,y a fixed ex ante 347, or a full year less documented downtime? The registered parameter box sits among the monitored parameters, monitoring frequency annual, and gives two sources in order of preference — operation sensor, or log of operation and maintenance. Its applied value is entered as “Estimate: 347 days”. v2.0 calls 347 “this conservative cap” for “relying on manual logs”. On the text the answer is min(347, days demonstrated by the log), which means the calendars can confirm or reduce the registered figure but never raise it. (b) Does the Improved Cooking precedent read across? That VPA computes technology days from its database and discounts recorded downtime — 8,579 days discounted from 13,715,217, 0.063% — which is the same construction. If it reads across, our calendars serve the same function. (c) Which version governs the 2026 monitoring period? The VPA is registered under v1.0; v2.0 enters into force about 7 October 2026; neither document contains any provision applying a new version to an already-registered activity before renewal, and the only transition clause, §17.1.1, operates at renewal. Full quotations, including §3.3.1 and §17.1.1 in full: docs/sdws27_basis.md. Note for the file: v1.0 and v2.0 say materially the same thing about DO, so the version question does not change the answer to (a).

Answered by James Walker (21 Sep 2026), not by Gold Standard: capped at 347 days without a sensor; actual days only for sensor-fitted pumps, sampled 50 per stratum, with the cap on the rest; a lost or damaged calendar is acceptable given the SOP, the visits and the call log. Written into calendar SOP v1.7, chapters 9 bis and 10.

Brief Ralf at Curtech on meter numbers versus calibration sample act-sensor-sample

closed 29 Sep 2026 Done: Ralf van Veenendaal was briefed by WhatsApp (Adriaan Mol, 29 Sep 2026).

Brief Ralf van Veenendaal at Curtech on the fleet-wide unit count and the calibration sample — they are two different numbers. Metering is fleet-wide. Per the StrokeMeter Technical Development Plan v1.2, Device A the Stroke Logger is “permanently mounted to a static part of every metered pump”, and production is sized for the whole metered fleet. The unit counts that stood here came from that plan, where illustrative counts briefed a supplier. They were never our register and have been removed — a figure on this page is a form response, a registered parameter or a named decision, never a number from a plan or a deck. What was removed is listed in docs/decision_log.md. The calibration sample is separate and much smaller: 50 pump calibrations a year, each a timed 5-minute discharge test against the meter installed on the pump, carried out with a small set of about 5 portable calibration pods (one of them a spare) moved from pump to pump. They are not the at least 100 permanently installed stroke meters (50 per stratum). Device B the Calibration Pod is that portable set, and the plan is explicit that pods “operate as sampling-campaign instruments… not as a fleet rotation”. The 90/10 sampling establishes litres per counted event — a fleet conversion factor per pump type — not which pumps are metered. Every pump is metered. This item previously read as a 60-unit sampled sensor deployment, which is not the architecture. The plan works to the 17 July 2026 census of 723 pumps; the register now reads 745 managed points, and the reconciliation is already an open action. The minimum-sample-size divergence between v1.0 and v2.0 bears on the calibration sample, not on the logger count.

Add the sample size to the brief. The sensor sample is 50 pumps per stratum, that is at least 100 StrokeMeters across Anosy and Maroantsetra (James Walker, 21 Sep 2026). Only those pumps can claim days operational above 347; the rest stay capped.

Get individual household consent, not only the village notice act-v2-nonclaimingClose the individual-level consent gap — the community-level notice is already in place. The point-of-use form does carry a consent question — A4, “Household consent obtained?” — but it is optional and conditional, and it holds 0 answers in 142 responses, while the Water Quality Testing Protocol makes obtaining consent a numbered step. Staff can follow the protocol exactly and leave no record. Fixing the field is a precondition for closing the gap, not a substitute for it. Found by the SOP/form conformance sweep, docs/sop_form_conformance.md D4. What we hold: the signed Community Agreement already carries the SDWS 20 notice word for word — “SaniTap a informé et notifié aux utilisateurs finaux qu’ils ne peuvent pas revendiquer de réductions d’émissions carbone du projet” — and v2.0 SDWS 20 accepts “Contracts with end-users” as a source, so the requirement is substantially met at community level. What we do not hold: Annexe B of the commune contract commits us to “preuves documentaires d’accord pour le transfert de propriété légale au niveau individuel”, and no individual record exists for any of the 732 carbon points. The point-of-use survey already carries a household consent question; it has been answered 0 times in 142 responses. Two decisions, in order. First, confirm whether the commune-level transfer satisfies the methodology on its own, given the Maire is “légitimement autorisé, au nom de la communauté” and the VPA-DD relies on the Mayor as the legally authorised Commune leader elsewhere. If it does, Annexe B is a commitment we have made and not kept — a contract-compliance matter, not a carbon-eligibility one. If it does not, the exposure is the whole portfolio, because the shortfall is identical everywhere. Second, either way, turn the existing consent question on and add the Annexe B transfer wording to it. Run the households-served survey and report its precision (SDWS 26) act-run-sdws-26-premisesRun the SDWS 26 premises-served survey, and report the precision actually achieved. Questions A9, A10 and A11 went live on the point-of-use form on 18 September 2026 and no responses exist yet. The parameter has no field instrument until this runs. Minimum 100 households at 90% confidence and 10% margin of error — but 100 is a floor, not a demonstration. The requirement is stated as “a sample size of 100 for a population greater than 1,000 does not inherently satisfy the 90/10 precision requirement… The CME must demonstrate in the VPA-DD that the actual precision level achieved using the observed data from the sample, specifically the actual proportion observed, and this must be validated by the Validation and Verification Body.” So calculate and report the achieved confidence interval from the observed proportion once the responses are in, and widen the sample if it does not meet 90/10. That requirement governs the survey regardless of the review's own state. The sample is drawn and reproducible. tools/draw_usage_sample.py draws it from the live register to the VPA-DD design — 90% confidence, 10% margin of error, at least 100 households and 8 clusters per scenario, Anosy and Maroantsetra separate — recording the seed, the extract date and the register checksum so it can be redrawn identically. Blocked by the instrument review: running a round on an instrument that is later changed wastes the round. The draw also reports five managed points in Androy that fall in neither named scenario — the Marolinta boreholes, outside the carbon fleet. They are reported for a decision, not assigned.

Source: INSTAT RGPH-3, census of June 2018 — the most recent official household size by region. • Anosy 4.3 (Tome 1, Tableau 26, p.41); Taolagnaro district 4.3 (Tome 2, Tableau 14, p.160); urban commune of Fort Dauphin 4.0 (Tome 2, Tableau 16, p.213). • Analanjirofo 3.6 (Tome 1, Tableau 26, p.41); Maroantsetra district 3.6 (Tome 2, Tableau 14, p.159); urban commune of Maroantsetra 3.3 (Tome 2, Tableau 16, p.195). EDS-V 2021 (household composition table) gives national 4.3, urban 4.0, rural 4.4 only. Comparison with the project survey, Nov 2025 (people per premises): • Fort-Dauphin 4.47: +0.17 (+4%) above Anosy and Taolagnaro; +0.47 (+12%) above Fort Dauphin town. • Maroantsetra 3.66: +0.06 (+2%) above Analanjirofo and the district; +0.36 (+11%) above Maroantsetra town. Census figures not scaled for growth (growth changes the number of households, not their size). The census counts ordinary households; the survey counts premises, which can hold more than one household. Files: Central Data Hub - Water Documents/Evidence/SDWS25 household size/ (RGPH-3 Tome 1 and Tome 2, RGPH-3 household characteristics report, TBSE Analanjirofo Dec 2025, EDS-V 2021 FR376). Refresh the mWater data before each report edition act-refresh-extractRefresh the mWater extract before each edition. The data this page is built from runs behind mWater, and the page now says by how much. The lag is measured each build by tools/check_freshness.py, which compares the newest date in the extract with the newest submission in mWater on the preventive maintenance, repair, call-centre and first-rehabilitation forms. Every count on this page describes the week the extract ends in, not the current week, so an old extract does not make the figures wrong — it makes them answer a question nobody asked. This closes itself when the lag reaches zero and reopens the moment it does not.

Settle the basis for the five-minute pump stroke test act-standardised-stroke-test-basisStandardised stroke test — the basis is settled. closed 18 Sep 2026 The standardised stroke test is SDWS 28 of ERSDWS V2, and the five-minute test is the accepted method pending the StrokeMeter. That is the basis we use. Published-text anomaly: Gold Standard published a version of ERSDWS containing a requirement to validate the stroke test against another method; that requirement was supposed to have been removed and does not reflect the agreed position. Recorded here so a verifier reading the published text and our file sees the discrepancy explained rather than discovered. A pump discharge test on a sample remains worth doing to establish litres per stroke, but it calibrates the StrokeMeter and does not on its own satisfy SDWS 23, which requires continuous monitoring. Source: James Walker, Head of Carbon, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 18 September 2026.

Brief Ralf at Curtech on meter numbers versus calibration sample act-sensor-sample

closed 29 Sep 2026 Done: Ralf van Veenendaal was briefed by WhatsApp (Adriaan Mol, 29 Sep 2026).

Brief Ralf van Veenendaal at Curtech on the fleet-wide unit count and the calibration sample — they are two different numbers. Metering is fleet-wide. Per the StrokeMeter Technical Development Plan v1.2, Device A the Stroke Logger is “permanently mounted to a static part of every metered pump”, and production is sized for the whole metered fleet. The unit counts that stood here came from that plan, where illustrative counts briefed a supplier. They were never our register and have been removed — a figure on this page is a form response, a registered parameter or a named decision, never a number from a plan or a deck. What was removed is listed in docs/decision_log.md. The calibration sample is separate and much smaller: 50 pump calibrations a year, each a timed 5-minute discharge test against the meter installed on the pump, carried out with a small set of about 5 portable calibration pods (one of them a spare) moved from pump to pump. They are not the at least 100 permanently installed stroke meters (50 per stratum). Device B the Calibration Pod is that portable set, and the plan is explicit that pods “operate as sampling-campaign instruments… not as a fleet rotation”. The 90/10 sampling establishes litres per counted event — a fleet conversion factor per pump type — not which pumps are metered. Every pump is metered. This item previously read as a 60-unit sampled sensor deployment, which is not the architecture. The plan works to the 17 July 2026 census of 723 pumps; the register now reads 745 managed points, and the reconciliation is already an open action. The minimum-sample-size divergence between v1.0 and v2.0 bears on the calibration sample, not on the logger count.

Add the sample size to the brief. The sensor sample is 50 pumps per stratum, that is at least 100 StrokeMeters across Anosy and Maroantsetra (James Walker, 21 Sep 2026). Only those pumps can claim days operational above 347; the rest stay capped.

Briefing drafted 26 Sep, awaiting send. The email “StrokeMeter: how many units, and how many for calibration” to Ralf at Curtech is in Adriaan's Drafts, not Sent Items (checked 26 Sep 2026). This item closes, citing that email, once it has been sent.

Source: James Walker, Carbon Lead, “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 2026-09-21: Sensors on a sample of 50 per stratum, to be safe; the actual days claimable for those 100, the cap on the rest.; Adriaan Mol (draft, not sent), “StrokeMeter: how many units, and how many for calibration”, 2026-09-26: Briefing drafted 26 Sep, awaiting send: at least 100 field units (50 per stratum); separately, a calibration sample of 50, each checked against a timed 5-minute discharge test once a year.

Check how accurately the calendars were machine-read act-complete-accuracy-assessment-calendarComplete the accuracy assessment of the calendar extraction. Manual transcription of the 50 selected calendars, against which the machine output is compared. The reference transcription is made by Adriaan Mol, who had seen the extraction’s aggregate error statistics but no per-cell output; that exposure is recorded in the method block of the calendar section so a verifier reads it alongside the agreement figure. Tell field teams: photograph the old calendar before replacing it act-calendar-custodyStanding rule, to be issued to every field team today: no calendar may be replaced until the previous one has been photographed and the photograph confirmed legible and uploaded. When a 2027 sheet is issued, the 2026 sheet stays at the water point. It is not removed, not taken away and not discarded. Sheets are replaced on a rolling basis — the SOP says so: “Les calendriers déjà posés sur le terrain restent au modèle 2024/2025 ; ils sont remplacés au fur et à mesure, sans campagne dédiée” — and a sheet that is gone cannot be re-photographed at any price. This rule was previously argued from a claim that 2027-dated sheets were being distributed nine months early. That claim was tested and does not hold — those sheets are in active use, not future stock. The rule stands on replacement happening at all, which it does. This is the precondition for the recovery round below — that round has nothing to photograph if the sheets have been thrown away first. The rule is written into SOP-MAD-SDWS27-CalendrierGardien as chapter 6 bis, added at v1.2 and carried forward unchanged into v1.3. What remains is issuing it to the teams, which is the part that protects sheets. The rule is deliberately stricter than “photograph it first”: the photograph must be confirmed legible and uploaded, because an illegible photograph of a discarded sheet is the same as no photograph.

Stays open (Adriaan Mol, 26 Sep 2026). The rule is confirmed unchanged in calendar SOP v1.7, chapter 6 bis.

Find out what the year printed on calendars is meant to mean act-printed-year-meaningEstablish what the year printed on a gardien calendar is meant to denote, and whether sheets are issued with a forward year deliberately. This is the key the whole days-operational evidence chain turns on. Coverage, the observable window, the locking of cells on the transcription page and the year-by-year emission-reduction attribution all derive from the printed year. It has been shown not to denote the period the sheet records: sheets printed 2027 were photographed during 2026 with the months already elapsed at the photograph marked far more often than the months after — they are in service, not held in stock. The analysis that measured this is not in this repository, so its counts and rates are not restated here. Two questions for the print run and the field: is the printed year the edition or print run of the sheet, or the period it is intended to cover; and are sheets with a forward year issued deliberately — a batch printed ahead and put straight into use — or by mistake. Template v1.4 removes our dependence on the answer; it does not supply it. New stock prints no year at all and the technician writes the period on the sheet, so from the January round forward the question stops mattering for new evidence. It still matters for the sheets already in the field, which is every sheet the retrospective years rest on, and only the print run and the field teams can say whether a forward year was deliberate. Consequence if the answer is “edition, not period”: the reader must key on something other than the printed year, and the published coverage figures move — bounded and small, water points with 2026 evidence going from 299 to 308 on the 2026-dated-sheet basis. That technical change follows from the answer and is not raised as a separate action until there is one. Best asked in the same conversation as the undatable-sheet list above.

Define what approving an mWater record means, and use it sparingly act-mwater-approval-policyDefine what approving an mWater record means, then apply it only where it buys something. Neither methodology version requires record approval. It is our own workflow, and that matters: a bulk approval by someone who has not read the records is worse than none, because it manufactures assurance a verifier may then rely on. The previous version of this item asked for a different, larger number of records to be approved. That count is withdrawn: it was carried forward from a superseded basis. That was the wrong ask.

What is worth doing: a documented quality check, against stated criteria, on a sample of the 1,464 unapproved old-combined-works records. Those carry the SDWS 2 eligibility evidence for the portfolio and they are a finite historical set — the form has taken one submission all year — so a sample can speak for the whole of it, and the criteria can be written down once.

Explicitly out of scope. Blanket approval of the ongoing weekly forms: approving records as they arrive adds a signature and no scrutiny, and it would have to be done for ever. The call-centre form (2,820 unapproved): a dispatch record carries no carbon quantity, decided 21 September 2026, so approving one asserts nothing about anything this page reports.

Owner is the work, not the database. Approving a works record is a judgement about whether the work was done and evidenced, which is Angelo’s and Jan’s to make. It is not an administrative right, and it should not sit with the mWater group administrator.

Photograph every surviving 2026 breakdown calendar at every pump act-2026-recoveryRun the 2026 calendar recovery round across the whole portfolio — not a sample. Photograph every surviving 2026 gardien calendar so 2026 becomes full-year evidence instead of partial. The denominator is all 732 carbon points — the actively managed register less Marolinta, computed every build, and coverage achieved is to be reported against that denominator and no other. Prioritise the 435 points with no dated 2026 sheet at all. The same round verifies that a calendar is physically present and legible at every point, which is a separate finding from whether it has been photographed — a point with no sheet on the wall needs a reissue, not a photograph. The round records the period at source, so attribution never depends on reading a printed header. Two steps, both before the shutter. First, the technician writes the year the sheet documents into the header, in pen — into the TAONA / ANNÉE box on v1.3 stock, or beside the pump identifier box on an older sheet — so the photograph itself carries the period. Second, the same year is entered as a field beside the photograph: a new whole-number question 2.15.7, “Année documentée par ce calendrier”, on the preventive-maintenance form de26d89a5c8a4452b42158c622be20d0, in question group d5233b2b immediately after 2.15.6, required whenever 2.15.6 carries an image. Where the year cannot be established from the sheet or from the gardien, the field is left empty and the period is treated as unproven — it is never filled in with the most likely year. Both steps are chapter 7 ter of the SOP. From the January round onward the period a sheet documents is recorded by the technician holding it, and is not inferred from the printed header. The question is live on the form as of 20 September 2026, id 3393e25651c047d0b8a29f34cdcf12d9, and is optional — stock already in the field carries no handwritten year, and a required field would force an invented answer. Making it required is a separate action below. The form carries French and English only, so the Malagasy wording — “Taona voarakitra amin’ity teti-andro ity” — leads the French label, as it does on the sheet itself; that too has its own action. Whole-portfolio, because the sampling question above is unsettled and the text leans against sampling the log; a sample would have to be redone if the answer is every point. Of 732 carbon points, 435 have no dated 2026 sheet at all. The tonnage and cash size of that gap is withdrawn with the per-year carbon basis it was computed from (act-carbon-year-basis) — the gap is those points, and it is evidence, not uplift: it protects the registered figure rather than exceeding it. A full-year 2026 record cannot be taken before 31 December 2026, by definition, so the round runs in January 2027. Field teams must be told immediately to leave the old sheet at the point when a new one is issued, and not to discard it. Replacement is rolling and continuous, so the evidence is at risk continuously rather than at a season. Feasibility is evidenced: sheets persist at points long after their year ends — 2024 sheets were still being photographed on 3 September 2026, twenty-one months later. Combine with the reissue round and the overdue preventive-maintenance round; the calendar is not a reason for a separate journey.

Have people transcribe calendars to check the machine reading act-transcription-roundRun the transcription validation round. 83 sheets are loaded and ready at the transcription page; 50 of them are machine-comparable and are the human-to-machine set, above the methodology minimum of 30. Report two agreement figures, not one. Per-day agreement, cell by cell over the observable window; and agreement on total days not operational per pump per period, which is the quantity SDWS 27 actually turns on — a reader can be wrong on individual days and right on the total, or the reverse, and only the second matters for the emission reduction. Run the households-served survey and report its precision (SDWS 26) act-run-sdws-26-premisesRun the SDWS 26 premises-served survey, and report the precision actually achieved. Questions A9, A10 and A11 went live on the point-of-use form on 18 September 2026 and no responses exist yet. The parameter has no field instrument until this runs. Minimum 100 households at 90% confidence and 10% margin of error — but 100 is a floor, not a demonstration. The requirement is stated as “a sample size of 100 for a population greater than 1,000 does not inherently satisfy the 90/10 precision requirement… The CME must demonstrate in the VPA-DD that the actual precision level achieved using the observed data from the sample, specifically the actual proportion observed, and this must be validated by the Validation and Verification Body.” So calculate and report the achieved confidence interval from the observed proportion once the responses are in, and widen the sample if it does not meet 90/10. That requirement governs the survey regardless of the review's own state. The sample is drawn and reproducible. tools/draw_usage_sample.py draws it from the live register to the VPA-DD design — 90% confidence, 10% margin of error, at least 100 households and 8 clusters per scenario, Anosy and Maroantsetra separate — recording the seed, the extract date and the register checksum so it can be redrawn identically. Blocked by the instrument review: running a round on an instrument that is later changed wastes the round. The draw also reports five managed points in Androy that fall in neither named scenario — the Marolinta boreholes, outside the carbon fleet. They are reported for a decision, not assigned.

Ask Gold Standard whether a stroke counter counts as a pump sensor act-sensor-definitionPut the sensor definition to Gold Standard. Ask whether a stroke counter constitutes an “operation sensor” for SDWS 27 (v1.0) / SDWS 32 (v2.0). Neither version defines the term — there is no definitions entry in either, and the phrase “monitoring device” appears nowhere in either document. But both versions connect the term to stroke counting in terms. v1.0 SDWS 23 Option 2: “Operation sensor measures directly operation time or pump stroke count”. And v2.0 SDWS 28 names them outright in its instrument row: “Operation sensors (e.g., stroke counters)”. So the residual question is narrower than it looked. v2.0 all but answers it; what is not written down is whether the same reading carries to the days-operational parameter — SDWS 27 in v1.0, which governs this crediting period and gives no such example — where the box says only “operation sensor”. This is the sole route to a days-operational figure above 347, on either version; if the answer is no, 347 is the ceiling for the life of the crediting period whatever the calendars show. Ask in the same letter as the SDWS 27 basis questions.

Confirm whether the new Gold Standard methodology (v2.0) applies to us act-confirm-whether-ersdws-v2Confirm whether ERSDWS v2.0 applies to this VPA before renewal. The VPA is registered under v1.0. v2.0 was published 9 July 2026 and §3.3.1 sets entry into force at “90 days from the publication date” — approximately 7 October 2026. §3.3 states no grandfathering for activities already registered under v1.0; the only transition-adjacent provision is §17.1.1, “at the renewal, the activity developer shall apply the latest version of this methodology available at the time of submission for renewal”. Parameter numbering differs between the versions — in v2.0 fNRB is SDWS 25 and the operation and maintenance log is SDWS 31 — so a v1.0-to-v2.0 parameter mapping is needed before any reading in this report can be carried across. Both versions, with checksums and retrieval date, are now in Water Documents/Methodology of record/.

Agree with Gold Standard how pump working days are evidenced (SDWS 27) act-sdws27-basisSettle the SDWS 27 basis with Gold Standard. Five questions, in one place, because they resolve together. (1) May the operation-and-maintenance log be demonstrated on a sample, or must it cover every water point? No sentence in either methodology version, or in the VPA-DD, settles this. But the text leans one way: the VPA-DD’s own sampling plan lists every parameter it intends to sample and SDWS 27 is absent; the sampling section is invoked from eight other parameter boxes in v1.0 and fifteen in v2.0 and from neither days-operational box; and the one express permission to sample anything under SDWS 27 attaches to the sensor route alone — “Operational sensors may be applied on a (90/10) sample basis”. We are planning on every point. (2) What happens to a point whose calendar is lost or illegible? Both documents are silent. “Illegible” and “missing” appear zero times in either; the four occurrences of “lost” in v2.0 are all “lost co-benefits” in the leakage sections. Exclusion, fallback to the registered estimate, or something else — there is no provision to quote. Our own SOP fills the gap with a conservative fallback, but that is a house rule no verifier is bound by, and it decides the treatment of 435 points. Then the three already open: (a) Is DOp,y a fixed ex ante 347, or a full year less documented downtime? The registered parameter box sits among the monitored parameters, monitoring frequency annual, and gives two sources in order of preference — operation sensor, or log of operation and maintenance. Its applied value is entered as “Estimate: 347 days”. v2.0 calls 347 “this conservative cap” for “relying on manual logs”. On the text the answer is min(347, days demonstrated by the log), which means the calendars can confirm or reduce the registered figure but never raise it. (b) Does the Improved Cooking precedent read across? That VPA computes technology days from its database and discounts recorded downtime — 8,579 days discounted from 13,715,217, 0.063% — which is the same construction. If it reads across, our calendars serve the same function. (c) Which version governs the 2026 monitoring period? The VPA is registered under v1.0; v2.0 enters into force about 7 October 2026; neither document contains any provision applying a new version to an already-registered activity before renewal, and the only transition clause, §17.1.1, operates at renewal. Full quotations, including §3.3.1 and §17.1.1 in full: docs/sdws27_basis.md. Note for the file: v1.0 and v2.0 say materially the same thing about DO, so the version question does not change the answer to (a).

Answered by James Walker (21 Sep 2026), not by Gold Standard: capped at 347 days without a sensor; actual days only for sensor-fitted pumps, sampled 50 per stratum, with the cap on the rest; a lost or damaged calendar is acceptable given the SOP, the visits and the call log. Written into calendar SOP v1.7, chapters 9 bis and 10.

Source: James Walker, Carbon Lead, “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 2026-09-21: Capped at 347 days without a sensor; actual days claimable only for sensor-fitted pumps, sampled 50 per stratum, with the cap on the rest; a lost or damaged calendar is acceptable given the SOP, visits and call log. Get individual household consent, not only the village notice act-v2-nonclaimingClose the individual-level consent gap — the community-level notice is already in place. The form cannot currently produce the evidence, which is why there is none. The point-of-use form does carry a consent question — A4, “Household consent obtained?” — but it is optional and conditional, and it holds 0 answers in 142 responses, while the Water Quality Testing Protocol makes obtaining consent a numbered step. Staff can follow the protocol exactly and leave no record. Fixing the field is a precondition for closing the gap, not a substitute for it. Found by the SOP/form conformance sweep, docs/sop_form_conformance.md D4. What we hold: the signed Community Agreement already carries the SDWS 20 notice word for word — “SaniTap a informé et notifié aux utilisateurs finaux qu’ils ne peuvent pas revendiquer de réductions d’émissions carbone du projet” — and v2.0 SDWS 20 accepts “Contracts with end-users” as a source, so the requirement is substantially met at community level. What we do not hold: Annexe B of the commune contract commits us to “preuves documentaires d’accord pour le transfert de propriété légale au niveau individuel”, and no individual record exists for any of the 732 carbon points. The point-of-use survey already carries a household consent question; it has been answered 0 times in 142 responses. Two decisions, in order. First, confirm whether the commune-level transfer satisfies the methodology on its own, given the Maire is “légitimement autorisé, au nom de la communauté” and the VPA-DD relies on the Mayor as the legally authorised Commune leader elsewhere. If it does, Annexe B is a commitment we have made and not kept — a contract-compliance matter, not a carbon-eligibility one. If it does not, the exposure is the whole portfolio, because the shortfall is identical everywhere. Second, either way, turn the existing consent question on and add the Annexe B transfer wording to it. Verbatim clauses and the mWater search: docs/enduser_consent_position.md. v2.0 also adds SDWS 18 and SDWS 19 on double counting; those are analytical and can be done at renewal. Divergence 6 in docs/methodology_version_map.md.

Update the stroke-test procedure to the new methodology's condition act-v2-stroke-testReconcile the stroke-test SOP with v2.0, which recognises it and adds a condition. v1.0 SDWS 23 offers a flow meter or an operation sensor and nothing else. v2.0 SDWS 28 Option 3 adds: “Alternative Methods (Handpumps only): If Options 1/2 are infeasible/inappropriate/prohibited, recognized methods/proxies (e.g., standardised stroke tests) are permitted. Requires robust justification and VVB validation. Measurement may be on a sampling basis.” This settles the numbering question standing in our own SOP — under v2.0 the stroke test is SDWS 28 Option 3, not SDWS 27 Option 3. The quarterly validation in that box does not reach us. It reads “For Option 3, the developer shall validate the proxy against a direct measurement (Option 1 or 2) quarterly” — expressly scoped to Option 3, and Option 2 is one of the direct measurements Option 3 is validated against. The frequency row confirms it: “Continuously (Options 1 & 2) or Periodically (Option 3/Sampling)”. The StrokeMeter logger is an Option 2 sensor, so the plan’s annual re-verification of the fleet conversion factor stands unchanged. The reconciliation is done in the stroke-test SOP v2.2 drafts (French and English): SDWS 28 Option 3 throughout, 50 pump calibrations a year, annual re-verification, and the five-minute test as the standardised test. Merged on 28 Sep 2026 into the SOP sign-off: nothing is left to reconcile, only to sign, so this item closes when the signed v2.2 is logged there.

Bring preventive maintenance visits back to the planned rate (SDWS 27) act-restore-preventive-maintenance-visitRestore the preventive-maintenance visit rate (SDWS 27). The calendar practice never lapsed: 758 of the 761 preventive-maintenance visits on record carry a calendar photograph, 720 of them on 2.15.6, the field of record. Calendar currency is therefore a function of how often a point is visited, not of whether the procedure is followed. Visits have collapsed: 100 in March 2026, 45 in July, 10 in August. Fort-Dauphin has had no preventive-maintenance visit since June 2026, and none in October or November 2025. The 62 points with no calendar photograph and the 385 stale beyond six months are the arithmetic consequence of that, not a field-discipline failure. Consequence: the SDWS 27 evidence base degrades as the visit rate falls. The value applied is 347 days, the default for a project without operation sensors, and the calendars are the operation and maintenance log that evidences it. A point whose log cannot be shown is not evidenced, so the claim weakens even where the pumps are working. Per-point list: gardien_calendar_coverage.csv.

Track how fast the call centre sends technicians and reports back act-repair-timeCall-centre response and report-back time — an operational performance target, explicitly not a carbon figure. This is a dispatch metric. The call centre exists to send a technician to a pump; the gardien calendar is the official record of days operational, decided 21 September 2026. Nothing in this item feeds a carbon calculation. Baseline, 21 September 2026. Recorded repairs then ran at a median of 1 day and a p90 of 16 days from notification to completion, across 187 repairs on 145 points; today the median is 1 day and the p90 12 days across 192 repairs. That is not the whole picture and cannot be: the repair form is created only once the work is finished — 143 of 187 records carried a completion date equal to the submission date — so the system cannot represent outstanding work at all. Counted from the call centre instead, 44 tickets were open with no repair recorded since, at a median 84 days, p90 193, longest 258; 21 had been open more than three months. Fort-Dauphin held 64% of that backlog on 17% of the points. Three things are asked for. (1) Clear the 44, oldest first, Fort-Dauphin first given the concentration — and note that clearing a ticket may mean recording a repair that already happened, not doing one. (2) A target on two intervals that are not currently measured at all: report to technician dispatch, and dispatch to report-back. The existing median of 1 day measures neither — it measures repairs that were completed and recorded, entered from memory at the moment of completion. Set the target on p90 rather than the median, because the median is already 1 day and the tail is where the time goes. (3) A way to represent a repair in progress, which the present form cannot do. Until that exists, an open ticket and an unreported repair are indistinguishable, which is the reason the 44 cannot be read as downtime. Merged, not duplicated: this item began as a repair-time target and now carries the call-centre response and report-back scope as well, under the same owner and deadline. It also carries the SOP amendment recording that the 95% pause rule is not applied. A dependency runs the other way too: whether those 44 tickets are stale or the calendars are under-marked is settled by the transcription round, not by this item.

Closes when manual — Adriaan marks it done: Adriaan marks the call-centre response target set.

Betanatanana — go and look at this well The type field is correct, and now confirmed from three photographs. 929469261 Grand puits Betanatanana is an open shaft dug into sand: no lining, no cover, no apron, no wellhead, no pump. The sides are bare earth with roots and vegetation growing down into the water; two loose planks and a cut branch lie across part of the mouth. A black HDPE pipe runs to it in two of the three photographs, which suggests it is being drawn from — so people may be drinking from it now. It cannot carry a safe-water claim in any form, and no correction to the record changes that: the type is right, the source is not improved. The open mouth sits at ground level in a walked area and is a fall hazard. No water quality record exists for it. Every sampling and result form in mWater was searched on 18 September — Clean Water sampling and result, Piped Water sampling and result — and not one references this point, so no SDWS 3 sample has ever been taken from it. The only record that does reference it is an unsubmitted draft on the borehole progress form, started 26 June 2026. Keep broken pumps in the register; never retire them for inactivity act-decommission-inactivity-fieldDecided 21 September 2026: SaniTap will not decommission or retire water points for inactivity. A pump that stays broken is a repair problem, not a register problem. It remains in the portfolio and is reported at its honest days operational. The reasoning is conservatism: removing under-performing points takes them out of the denominator and flatters the fleet average — the worst points leave the register and the reported availability of what remains rises, without a single pump working better. That is the less conservative treatment and the one a verifier would question. It is also what the methodology already assumes: neither version has any provision for a retired supply, because DOp,y is days operational and a pump that stops working simply contributes fewer of them. What follows: the 95% pause rule in the French suppression SOP is not applied and that SOP should be amended to say so; the permanent-deletion criteria are untouched, none of them being an availability judgement; no writable status property is needed in the register, because the only thing it was wanted for was a “paused” state that no longer exists, and the ZZ TEST name convention already handles the two records that are not water points; and repair speed becomes the only lever on days operational, which is why time to repair is now a headline metric above. Decision record, with the analysis that led to it: docs/decommissioning_rule_question.md. The original finding stands — the “jours d’inactivité” field exists on no live form — and is now moot for retirement, though the SOP amendment is not. Neither SOP is obsolete. Both carry permanent-deletion criteria that have nothing to do with availability — duplicate records, confirmed persistent contamination, irreparable or abandoned infrastructure, serious health or safety risk, a point taken over by another funder, no access — and all of those remain live. What is superseded is the 95% pause rule in the French SOP alone, which the English one never carried. That one clause should be struck; the documents stay.
