Portfolio by partner

Who operates what, and where each figure comes from. The three bases are not reconciled to each other and are not the same objects.

SaniTapCarbon programme owner · VPA GS12601

SaniTap holds the Gold Standard project and the carbon file. The carbon figures on this page are reported against the SaniTap carbon portfolio, the Maroantsetra and Fort-Dauphin pumps; the portfolio headline figures also take in Marolinta and Endur’O, which are outside it. The operators below deliver the work.

MadAvanceHand pumps · Maroantsetra, Fort-Dauphin, Marolinta

MadAvance figures are computed from mWater at each build. The 745 actively managed hand pumps, their maintenance record and their calendars are all MadAvance operations, and everything in the days-operational chain below rests on them.

Endur’OPiped systems · register readable since 16 Sep 2026

Endur’O’s mWater group was opened to us on 16 September 2026, so their register is now readable and is reported here beside the agreed programme numbers. Read the Endur’O column as two separate bases, each with its source.

First monitored volume — Endur’O smart meter

The first smart meter is installed and reporting, on an urban Endur’O system in Antananarivo. This is the first monitored-volume data the programme has produced: until now every volume figure in this report has been modelled or asserted, not measured.

It matters beyond the one site. Metered volume is parameter SDWS 23 — the measurement that lets Method 1 close rather than rest on defaults, and the basis for SDWS 27, days operational, which until now has had no measured input at all. One meter does not close either parameter; it establishes that the measurement exists and can be read.

Days operational on piped systems and kiosks is assessed per system, not per tap. Outlets of the same system within 1 km of one another form one service unit, so one tap down while the next one delivers is not a day lost. On metered sites the metered volume is expected to be the binding term in Qy = min(Qm, Qpop): metered customers are not expected to pay for water for animals, gardens or washing, as they draw it from a hand pump. James Walker, 23 September 2026. Hand pumps are unchanged.

How the service unit is defined for piped systems and kiosks

Radius: 1 km. Outlets of the same system within this distance of one another form one service unit, and days operational is assessed for the unit, not for each tap. Source: James Walker, Carbon Lead, email “Re: Days operational: we are applying a hand-pump rule to multi-tap sites”, 23 Sep 2026 — “Uptime / functionality is at a per system level” and “1km. Easier to define radius on a map and less subjective.”

What counts as one system. Each Antananarivo kiosk draws either from the Jirama mains or from its own local borehole, so each kiosk is its own system and service unit. On other piped systems the smart taps draw from the system; the system is the unit. Source: Adriaan Mol, 25 Sep 2026.

Who can use them. Kiosks are always public. Other piped systems have a very small number of private connections. Hand pumps are unchanged by any of this.

How the Moramanga piped-water baseline is used

Baseline fuel consumption is not measured. Emission reductions are worked out from the theoretical energy needed to boil 1 litre of water for 5 minutes and the efficiency of the baseline cooking device. The baseline survey’s stove question is therefore an input, because it gives the device; no fuel quantity is to be collected, and none is an open question.

Whether households actually boil does not change the credit value. The market does not recognise it. Boiling answers in the baseline survey are descriptive only.

Source: James Walker, Carbon Lead, email “Re: Moramanga carbon baseline: 331 households, and the boiling numbers”, 23 Sep 2026 — “The meth does not measure baseline fuel consumption” and “the presence of actually boiling does not increase the value of the credits”. Survey: Piped Water || Baseline Cbn, 3ef4385a619244c7ad129169ac1ec71f.

Whose dashboard this is. The readings are published by Endur’O on an Endur’O dashboard — open the live meter dashboard. Direct data access has been requested so the readings can enter our own evidence chain and be carried in the monitoring file, rather than being viewed through a third-party link. Until that access is granted, treat the dashboard as a sighting of the data, not as evidence on file.

Water quality on the piped systems — SDWS 3

Managed piped systems: 1. A piped system joins the managed portfolio when its rehabilitation works are complete and its post-rehabilitation water-quality tests are done; 1 was admitted by decision instead — the first Antananarivo smart-tap kiosk, operational with SaniTap/Curtech meters and its data in Zoho. The managed piped figures hold 0 water-quality results, 0 of them at or below 0 CFU per 100 mL: 1 managed system has no water-quality test on record yet — a test at the kiosk’s dispensing point is on the action list. 4 systems have their upgrade or new build under way and 20 Endur’O water systems are not managed.

Pre-project baseline, for systems whose upgrade or new build is under way — the evidence of need. These results establish the starting situation that qualifies a system for the programme; they describe the water before the works and count toward no managed figure. 43 baseline results sit on Amboasary gara, in 5 sampling rounds between March 2026 and August 2026: 38 exceed 0 CFU per 100 mL and 5 do not — median 3, highest 50 CFU per 100 mL — and free residual chlorine read zero in 42 of the 43 where it was measured. The water is unsafe at baseline. 0 of these results record which tap was sampled; that is required of every post-rehabilitation result.

2 further results on the piped form name a MadAvance hand pump, 742895333, as their water system: they belong on the hand-pump result form, and re-entering them there is on the action list.

Results paired with their samples: 0 of 0; 0 flagged for pairing by hand

The rule. Piped water quality is sampled only at public standposts and kiosks: what comes out of the tap. No source, tank or household samples. A result on the piped result form pairs with the most recent unpaired record on the piped sampling form at the same water point (sampling 1.1b), taken within the 72 hours before the result was submitted. Each sample pairs once. A pair takes its GPS, sample type and photo from the sampling record. The sampling date on the result (1.2.2) is a cross-check only: more than 1 day from the sample keeps the pair and adds a date-mismatch note. The code and GPS copied onto the result (1.2.1, 1.2.3) are not read. A sample with no water point, or at a household, is outside protocol and is flagged, never paired. A sample at an earlier-project record (another organisation’s old kiosk) pairs through the Moramanga crosswalk and counts, flagged to use the Endur’O point next time. Decision: Adriaan Mol, 28 Sep 2026.

How the piped water-quality figures are worked out

Source. Piped Water || Water Quality Testing_SDWS 3__Result (0ac68d8274d24f54af0c28b29119b77d), all 46 responses, extracted 2026-10-07; each names its water system, and every Endur’O water system (25, extracted 2026-10-07) has a status in data/piped_systems_status.json: managed, upgrade or new build under way, or not managed. The build fails if mWater holds a system the file does not list.

Status. The 4 systems whose upgrade or new build is under way are Amboasary gara, Ambohibola, Amboanjo, Andilanatoby — the Moramanga piped systems, the ones the Moramanga carbon baseline survey and the Moramanga piped water-point identification both name. They are Deichmann-funded; some are existing systems being upgraded, their taps already in use, and some are being built from scratch (Source: Adriaan Mol, September 2026; docs/piped_system_model.md.) Status: upgrade or new build under way: works are not complete and post-rehabilitation tests have not happened. Antananarivo sites are managed only once onboarded: the first smart-tap kiosk (water system 1125843376, water point 1125843383, Antsahakely) was admitted to the managed portfolio by decision, from its operational date, 14 September 2026 — the date of commissioning recorded on its mWater registration. Once the Curtech dispensing-events feed exists, the build re-derives the date as the first non-test dispense on the kiosk’s device — test shopkeepers SK01 and SK02 and test cards excluded — and this note names that dispense as its source. No water-quality test is yet on record for it. The other Antananarivo sites are not yet onboarded and stay outside. Source: Adriaan Mol, 25 Sep 2026.

The join rule, and why baseline never counts. A piped system joins the managed portfolio only when its rehabilitation works are complete and its post-rehabilitation water-quality tests are done (Adriaan Mol, 25 Sep 2026). The build applies it by date: once a system’s works-completion date is recorded, its results dated after it are post-rehabilitation and count, and the system moves to managed on the next build that holds one; its results on or before that date are baseline and never count, whatever happens to the system later. A system admitted by decision is managed from its operational date and the same line applies: only its results after that date count. A result’s date is its sampling date, else its result date, else the day it was submitted.

Meeting the rule. E. coli is question 1.4, recorded in CFU per 100 mL; a result meets the rule at or below the threshold the hand-pump figures use. Computed every build by tools/rebuild_piped_wq.py; the rule is proved on doctored status files by tools/test_piped_wq.py.

The Endur’O estate, reconciled — three lists, one disposition per site

Three lists claimed to describe one estate and disagreed. This is the single disposition per site, and where the Endur’O count on this page comes from. 131 sites.

The three lists. Coddy’s 128 Sites KML — which actually holds 131 points — is an exact subset of the earlier 157-point 13 Août file: every one of the 131 matches a 13 Août row on both name and coordinates. The 26 points dropped between them are all FAHASOAVANA. Against those sit the 111-point UNICEF list — every one of its points is in the table below, as 92 matched, 2 duplicate and 17 retired — and the Endur’O mWater group. Sites were matched on proximity within 250 m, never on name: the lists spell the same places differently (MALEBITSY / MALEBITSY CENTRE), so a name join both misses real matches and invents false ones.

131 is the Endur’O programme-site count, and it comes from one file. It stands on the Endur’O card and in no managed figure: these sites are not in the managed portfolio, which counts a piped system only when its status in data/piped_systems_status.json is “managed” (Adriaan Mol, 5 Oct 2026). Every Endur’O figure above is computed from data/enduro_disposition.csv, which carries the evidence for each site: which lists it appears in, the matched name in each, the distance, and whether mWater holds it. Earlier editions of this page said 138 and 111 in different places as counts of Endur’O sites; both are withdrawn as site counts. The UNICEF list reconciled in this section is a different list that happens to be the same size.

Two things this does not settle. Only 4 of the 131 sites are in the Endur’O mWater group, so the register and the map are still separate universes — the count is Coddy’s KML, not a live mWater figure, and cannot yet be refreshed automatically. And the duplicate pair is unresolved: if they are one site the count is 130. Neither the 131 programme sites nor any figure derived from them has entered a carbon calculation or a managed figure, and it should not until Coddy confirms the boundary.

The operator convention — how MadAvance and Endur’O assets are told apart
How MadAvance and Endur’O assets are told apart — the operator convention

The rule: operator is mWater group membership, never water point type. A record belongs to MadAvance if its _managed_by is the MadAvance group, and to Endur’O if it is the Endur’O group c305b9b8…. Nothing else decides it, with one recorded exception: 742896839 is a managed MadAvance pump whose tag reads all, and is counted while its tag is corrected (on the action list; see “Map count versus register count”).

Why type cannot do this job: the categories are not disjoint. Endur’O will hold hand pumps as its estate grows. MadAvance already holds Canzee, India Mark and the Marolinta boreholes — three different types, one operator. And a kiosk and a tapstand can share a type while belonging to different operators. Type describes the hardware; it has never described who maintains it.

alt_id_org is a secondary label only. It is useful for reading a record and for tracing provenance — water point 742896839 carries alt_id_org: MadAvance while its group membership is wrong, which is exactly how that error was found. But it is a label, not the rule: it is free text, it is not enforced, and it is not what any query filters on. Where operator is meant, group membership is the test.

tools/check_consistency.py asserts that no figure on this page is derived from water point type where operator is what is meant.

How the people-served figure is built

MadAvance hand pumps only. Endur’O piped systems carry their own beneficiary figures and are not in this calculation. SDWS 1 needs a defensible number, and this is the method of record: WorldPop, not the roof-count census.

What the registered VPA-DD says about SDWS 1
What the registered VPA-DD says

SDWS 1 is a parameter fixed ex ante — the VPA-DD carries it in section B.6.2, Data and parameters fixed ex ante, “recorded for each CWT/CWS installation ex-ante at the time of start of crediting period. In case of progressive installation — for new CWT/CWS units before 1st issuance for new units.”

The registered measurement method names WorldPop. From the parameter box, Source of data: “The Project will use a digital tool to calculate the number of households and institutions per CWS. This may involve satellite imagery and population data. The methodology is in development and may be changed throughout the crediting period as new techniques are developed. One method which may be used is WorldPop raster data for the 1km radius around the project water point, or the Meta Data for Good high resolution population density maps in conjunction with the mWater Population Density Overlay tool.” Under Choice of data or Measurement methods and procedures: “Data measurement will use the most accurate determination of household count. For example, this may be WorldPop raster data or the mWater Population Density Overlay based on each individual water source using the precise GPS location data…”

The rooftop figure is the ex ante average, not the measured value. Same box, Value(s) applied: “Ex-ante average of 32.5 households per CWS is based on initial assessment of 4,310 water sources using satellite imagery”, and Measurement methods: “Ex-ante average uses rooftop count using satellite imagery.” WorldPop on a 1 km radius is what this report applies, and it is a registered measurement method. The roof-count census below is a cross-check, not the figure of record.

Footnote — where the ex ante figures come from
Footnote — where the ex ante figures come from, and why the measured value differs

The two ex ante figures. SDWS 1 applies 32.5 households per CWS, stated in the box as an average from an “initial assessment of 4,310 water sources using satellite imagery”. SDWS 26’s additional comment registers district values instead — “Estimated premises per CWS: Anosy: 31, Maroantsetra: 37” — on a build-out of 1,000 water points, 200 in Anosy and 800 in Maroantsetra. Weighted 200/800 those give 35.8 households, not 32.5.

Both reduce to one number. The ex ante ER calculator derives people per source directly: 88,783 users recorded on mWater over 636 water points = 139.6 people per CWS, and 20,647 households over the same 636 = 32.5. The district pair reproduces the same 139.6 divided by district household size — 139.6 ÷ 4.5 = 31.0 for Anosy, 139.6 ÷ 3.7 = 37.7 for Maroantsetra, entered as 37. So 32.5 and 35.8 are the same population estimate divided by different household sizes: a blended 4.3 in one case, 4.5 and 3.7 in the other, plus the rounding of 37.7 down to 37.

What could not be established. The figure of 4,310 water sources appears once in the VPA-DD, in that one sentence, with no geography stated and no supporting annex. It does not match the 636 water points the calculator divides by. The two cannot be reconciled from the documents, and no cause is offered here for the difference.

Measured against ex ante. Maroantsetra measures 139 people per point against 136.9 ex ante, a 2% difference. Fort-Dauphin measures 317 against 139.5. The gap is settlement density, not the capacity caps. Before capping, the WorldPop allocation averages 594 people per point in Fort-Dauphin with 74 of 128 points at the pump ceiling, against 140 in Maroantsetra with 3 of 604 capped, and 0 in Marolinta — 76 capped pumps in all. Capping already removes about half the modelled population in Fort-Dauphin and what remains is still 2.3× the ex ante average. The ex ante value is a single programme-wide average struck before measurement; the registered source of data provides for measuring each source with the most accurate tool available, so a per-point measurement departing from that average is expected rather than anomalous.

From first rehabilitation to the pumps we maintain today

Where each figure comes from, so that "how many water points do we have?" has one answer. Everything below is computed from mWater on the night of issue.

The carbon fleet has not grown through new work since 1 January 2026. The maintained fleet stood at 736 until 23 September — the carbon fleet is the same pumps less Marolinta, 732 today — when one point joined through a record correction rather than new work: 742894057, a Fort-Dauphin Canzee first rehabilitated in April 2024, whose register name had not been a pump model.

Work has been done, and it is not carbon work. The rehabilitation and new construction recorded this year is Marolinta — Deichmann-funded and deliberately outside the carbon programme. It is logged on the borehole-progress form, which does not capture SDWS 2 evidence, and that is the right form for uncredited work: there is no reason to collect eligibility evidence for points that are not being credited. 1 of the 14 points on that form are not in our portfolio — the form has two deployments, 13 points in Marolinta and 1 in Moramanga, and only 13 of them all is a point we maintain. And there is a second reason, which is not about recording discipline at all. The first-rehabilitation branch of the old combined form was retired, and a dedicated successor (Première réhabilitation) was deployed to three districts. It has never received a single response. So "no first rehabilitation recorded this year" is not a team forgetting to write things down: the form they were told to use is empty, and the form they used to use no longer takes records. Every population on this page now reads the retired form, the successor and the Marolinta borehole form together, so the first response on the successor enters the fleet rather than vanishing.

One consequence worth recording. If Marolinta were ever brought into the carbon programme, the SDWS 2 evidence would not exist retrospectively — the three-month non-operational record, the local representative’s confirmation and the success verification are captured at the time or not at all. That is a note for a future decision, not a gap in the present evidence chain. Why the carbon fleet has not grown sits with the Head of Carbon; reconciling the Marolinta count is Deichmann reporting.

Against what Jan reported in the SLT minutes of 14 September 2026: 10 new boreholes and 10 rehabilitations to date. Two different bases, which must not be added or compared. The 3,130 above is a field count: the sum of the beneficiaries the team recorded on each of the 13 records, 150–300 per point. Marolinta sits outside the carbon programme, the field count is the honest number for the works on this form, and the 13 points lie within about a kilometre of each other — so summing per-point service areas without the model’s overlap split would double-count badly. All 13 carry a usable coordinate; none was excluded for want of one.

No Marolinta point carries a preventive visit, a repair or a water-quality result. Not one of the 13 has any maintenance or testing record of any kind, so none can enter the carbon file however the works are recorded. How to read these figures, and what they cannot show

Read the median with care: it measures repairs that happened, and nothing else. All 192 final responses carry both a notification date and a completion date, and 146 of them give a completion date equal to the day the form was submitted. The form is created at the moment the repair is finished, so a repair in progress has no record and the dates are entered from memory by the technician closing it. 60% of repairs record no more than a day and 69% record the breakdown and the notification on the same day. These figures cannot show a backlog, because nothing enters this table until it is already fixed. 192 repairs across 147 water points: carbon points, except those in the table’s row for points outside the managed register; the trend to watch is p90, which moved 1 → 4 → 35 → 9 days over the last four quarters.

Tickets left open are long, and that is a report-back problem before it is anything else. At the 21 September baseline 44 points had a call-centre contact whose latest answer to “is the pump currently working?” was no, with no repair completed since; the list below carries 31 today. The two are not counted the same way, so the drop is not tickets closed: the baseline took any call, however old, whose latest answer was no and had no completed repair after it; the list below takes down-reports since 2026-03-01 and closes one on any repair record dated on or after it, on either repair source. A ticket that stays open means the report-back did not arrive, not that the pump is still broken. At that baseline: median 84 days open, p90 193, longest 258; 33 open more than a month, 21 more than three months, 11 more than six. By district: 28 Fort-Dauphin, 16 Maroantsetra — Fort-Dauphin carries 128 of the 745 managed points and held 64% of the backlog. A further 172 points last answered “partially” working, which is neither counted here nor nothing.

No carbon quantity is attached to any of this. An open ticket is not a day not operational: it means the report-back did not arrive. The figures on this panel are operational measures of dispatch and report-back, and nothing here feeds a carbon calculation. What repair speed is worth for carbon is set out in the days-operational section: 347 days is the ceiling for every pump without an operation sensor, calendar or not, so faster repair cannot raise the figure — what it does is keep 347 from being cut, which is the condition the calendars exist to test.

Mapping rules: how the 1 km service area is drawn

What parameter SDWS 1 requires, what this report does about each requirement, and where we are not yet compliant. Stated here so it is on the record rather than discovered at verification.

RequirementWhat this report doesStatus
1 km service area, demonstrated by satellite imaging or GPS coordinatesEvery water point carries a GPS fix in the mWater register. The service area is a 1 km buffer computed on a local equidistant projection, so the radius is a true 1,000 m on the ground rather than a degree approximation.applied
No double counting between neighbouring water pointsWhere service areas overlap, the population in the overlap is divided equally between every water point that reaches it. A cell reachable from three pumps contributes one third to each. Nobody is counted twice.applied
Insurmountable barriers — end users on the far side shall be excludedApplied. Coastline, rivers and canals form the barrier network, minus any reach carrying a bridge or a ford, since the methodology requires the barrier to be insurmountable. Only the polygon fragment containing the pump is kept; the barrier lines are drawn 50 m past the circle before it is cut, so a river crossing the circle always divides it (fixed 30 Sep 2026, see the note). The method is one script, sdws1_population.py, run by this report and by the UNICEF selection tool from the private repository SaniTap-water/sdws1-method at commit f2e2004; the script, its inputs' checksums, the per-point outputs and the sensitivity runs are in the evidence folder. 628 of 745 points have at least one barrier transecting their circle; 366 lose more than a tenth of their service area.applied
Capacity ceiling as a conservativeness safeguardReported population is min(allocated, pump capacity): Canzee 500, India Mark 300.applied
Survey households must lie inside the 1 km radiusThe sampler draws only from registered water points and the field rule selects households walking out from the source. The barrier constraint must be added to the sampler when the clip is built.partial → open action
How the 1 km service area is drawn, and how we comply — the full method

The rule, as written. Gold Standard, Emission reductions from Safe Drinking Water Supply v1.0, parameter SDWS 1: “End users premises (e.g. households, institutions) within 1 km distance of project water source or a total collection time of 30 minutes or less for a round trip, including queuing, using the travel modes of walking or pedaling. … If there are any insurmountable barriers (e.g. river without bridge) transecting the circle defined by the 1 km radius or 30 mins distance, then end-users on the far side of the barrier shall be excluded from the count.”

Why the overlap rule matters more here than the barrier rule. In Maroantsetra the water points sit very close together: every one of the 604 has at least one neighbour whose service area overlaps its own, the average point overlaps 28 others, the most crowded overlaps 59, and 1,205 pairs of pumps in the portfolio stand within 200 m of each other. After the barrier clip and the equal split, the average Maroantsetra point is allocated 140 people and only 3 of 604 reach the capacity ceiling — so in Maroantsetra the figure is set by the overlap rule, not by the cap. Fort-Dauphin is the opposite: an average allocation of 594 with 74 of 128 points capped. This is also why the two sites diverge against the roof count in opposite directions.

Equal splitting is a choice, and it is the choice that reports the highest total. The methodology requires only that nobody is counted twice; it does not prescribe how to divide a shared population. Dividing equally ignores the fact that a household usually walks to its nearest pump, so a distance-weighted or nearest-source assignment would be more realistic. It would not, however, raise the reported total. The population inside the service areas is fixed, so any rule that divides it differently moves people between pumps without changing the sum — it can only change the total through the capacity ceiling, and concentrating people onto fewer points pushes more of them above that ceiling, where the excess is discarded. An earlier edition of this page stated the opposite; that was wrong. Equal splitting is retained for now because it is simple to state and simple to reproduce, and the nearest-source and inverse-distance-weighted variants have now been run alongside it. On the raster of record, without barriers, equal reports 129,018, inverse-distance-weighted 128,106 and nearest-source 124,381; with the barrier clip, 125,710, 124,966 and 121,709 — confirming that a more realistic allocation lowers the reported total rather than raising it. The comparison is filed in the evidence library. These variant runs are dated 2026-10-01, over the fleet as it stood that day and after the barrier split fix. The figure of record, 125,710, is the equal split with the barrier clip from the same run (2026-10-01).

Where the allocation rule does matter. It sets the people-per-pump figure, which drives maintenance cost per credit — 139 people per pump in Maroantsetra against 317 in Fort-Dauphin. And it governs how a monitored-volume sample must be stratified: a pump in a ten-pump village and a standalone pump are not interchangeable.

Who is counted as served: the annual usage survey

The 1 km service area answers parameter SDWS 1 — who lives near enough. It does not answer parameter SDWS 26 — who actually draws water from our pump. These are different numbers and the methodology asks for both.

RequirementWhere we standStatus
Sampling frame — a complete, randomisable list of water pointsThe mWater register is the frame. Every actively managed point carries a code, a GPS fix and an administrative chain, so a random draw is reproducible from the register alone.in place

What parameter SDWS 26 requires, and how the usage survey is sampled — the full method

The rule, as written. Gold Standard, Emission reductions from Safe Drinking Water Supply v1.0, parameter SDWS 26, HHp,y — number of premises served: a survey of the premises within 1 km of the project water source, checking how often each used the project water source during the year. Only premises reporting use at least every two days may be counted. Annual.

It is a sample, not a census. Surveying every household around 745 hand pumps is neither required nor possible. The registered validated project activity design document for this programme sets the method: the project database drives a digital randomisation tool that randomly selects the water points to be visited for the annual monitoring survey; end users at those points are then selected by the random-walk method, by random selection of premises from rooftop satellite imagery, or by another representative and unbiased method. The survey must reach a 90% confidence interval with a 10% margin of error, minimum 100 households. Parameter SDWS 26 is reported as a mean (premises served per water point) together with the proportion reporting use at least every two days.

What this means for the figures on this page. The people-served number here is a modelled residential population inside the service areas. It is the SDWS 1 boundary count, and it is the right basis for planning and for this report. It is not the SDWS 26 figure, and the SDWS 26 figure will be lower, because it counts only premises that report using the pump at least every other day. The two are reconciled by the usage survey, not by the model.

Parameter SDWS 25 — people per premises
How people per premises is derived — INSTAT RGPH-3

People per premises is taken from INSTAT RGPH-3, rural stratum, 4.3 persons per household. That is the external source for monitoring; the VPA-DD’s registered ex-ante values (4.5 Anosy, 3.7 Maroantsetra) came from the project survey, and the 2025 round’s own household sizes, which still round to them, are in the SDWS 26 section. National is 4.2 and urban 3.9. Source: RGPH-3 Thème 4, INSTAT, February 2021, Résumé p. XXI. The same figure appears in RGPH-3 Tome 1, Tableau 26, p. 41, which is now in the evidence folder.

The source choice has to be justified. Three national sources disagree: INSTAT RGPH-3 gives 4.2 national and 4.3 rural, MICS-6 (2018) gives 4.5 and EDSMD-V (2021) gives 4.3. That is a spread of about 7% on a figure that multiplies straight through the people-served total, so the choice must be justified in the design document rather than assumed. The regional figures matter more than the spread: Analanjirofo rural is 3.6, and it holds 604 of the 745 points, so using the national rural 4.3 there overstates people per premises by roughly 19%. Which figure the model should use — national rural or regional rural — is an open decision, not a settled one.

Annual independent cross-check, 7 Oct 2026. The 2025 round of the project survey (November 2025) measured 4.47 people per premises in Fort-Dauphin and 3.66 in Maroantsetra. Against the most recent official figures for the same places:

  • Anosy (Fort-Dauphin): region 4.3, Taolagnaro district 4.3, urban commune of Fort Dauphin 4.0. The survey is +0.17 (4%) above the region and district and +0.47 (12%) above the town.
  • Analanjirofo (Maroantsetra): region 3.6, Maroantsetra district 3.6, urban commune of Maroantsetra 3.3. The survey is +0.06 (2%) above the region and district and +0.36 (11%) above the town.

Every official figure is from INSTAT RGPH-3 (census of June 2018): region from Tome 1, Tableau 26, p. 41; district from Tome 2, table 14 (Maroantsetra p. 159, Taolagnaro p. 160); commune from Tome 2, table 16 (Maroantsetra p. 195, Fort Dauphin p. 213). Nothing newer gives a figure by region. The INSTAT Tableau de Bord Socio-Économique for Analanjirofo (December 2025, Tableau 4, PDF p. 20) reprints the 2018 census sizes, printing 3.5 for the region where the census counts themselves round to 3.6; no December 2025 edition exists for Anosy. EDS-V 2021 gives only national (4.3), urban and rural sizes. The census figures are used as published and are not scaled to 2025: population growth changes the number of households, not their size. The survey counts people per premises and the census people per ordinary household, so a premises holding more than one household reads higher in the survey. Sources in Central Data Hub - Water Documents/Evidence/SDWS25 household size/; closes act-find-source-annual-independent.

Household water quality (SDWS 18, share of samples passing)

Whether the water is still safe in the household, not only at the pump. The 2025 round tested 140 households in November and December 2025, on the household water-quality survey in mWater. A household (point-of-use) sample passes at fewer than 10 E. coli per 100 ml, the WHO low-risk band (Water Quality Protocol v2.1 section 5.1; methodology v2.0 §3.2.3.2); a pump or tap sample would pass only at 0. All 140 are household samples.

Water point and Household: the mWater codes the record is linked to. The 2026 round: sampling design and field protocol
The 2026 round: sampling design and field protocol
  • Sampling frame. The 745 water points in the maintained portfolio. A point is eligible if it has a final SDWS 3 result passing the health-based rule (Escherichia coli 0 per 100 ml; arsenic ≤ 10 µg/L; fluoride ≤ 1.5 mg/L; nitrate ≤ 50 mg/L and manganese ≤ 0.08 mg/L where measured), is not abandoned, and is not in Beloha district (Marolinta, which sits outside the carbon programme). pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity and iron never disqualify a source. The eligible count in each stratum — HP-FD (Fort-Dauphin / Anosy) and HP-MA (Maroantsetra) — is computed by the sampler at draw time, from mWater, and recorded on that round’s sampling record; this page cannot apply the chemical limits itself, so it does not restate the count.
  • Design. Two-stage cluster sample: 12 sources drawn with probability proportional to size (PPS) across communes, plus 20 % replacements, then 5 households per source selected in the field by the k-th-household walking rule. Design effect DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC, where ICC is the intra-cluster correlation; at ICC 0.1 that is 1.4, so a nominal 60 samples gives an effective sample size of about 43.
  • The sampler. A purpose-built draw tool, sanitap-sampler, reads the frame live from mWater, applies the eligibility rule, performs the PPS draw and emits a signed sampling record. This is the instrument that makes the draw reproducible rather than discretionary.
  • Reproducibility. The random seed is the round name plus the stratum (for example 2026R1-HP-FD). The same seed against the same frame reproduces the identical draw, which has been verified on the deployed tool. A validation and verification body (VVB) can therefore re-run our draw rather than take it on trust.
  • Audit record. Each round is filed append-only under records/<round>/<stratum>/ as a sampling-record PDF with the machine-readable audit trail embedded as an attachment, alongside the selection in Excel and comma-separated values (CSV). No water point coordinates are ever published in these records.
  • Field reach rule. A drawn source more than 25 km from every other selected source and from the district town is flagged; it may be replaced in the field only if genuinely unreachable, and the reason is recorded on the sampling record.
  • Link to the laboratory record. The record identifier (which is the seed) is entered on every point-of-use and point-of-collection response in mWater, so each household result joins back to the draw that selected it.
  • Field protocol. The mWater point-of-use survey follows Annex B of water quality protocol v2.2: test type (point of use, point of collection, blank, duplicate, positive control), consent, container and spout condition, sample collection, filling and transport, processing, incubation reading, result and supervisor review. Pass thresholds: E. coli < 10 per 100 ml at point of use and < 1 per 100 ml at point of collection and for blanks.

Open before the 2026 round (on the action list): field blanks, duplicates and a paired pump sample, which the 2025 round did not have, and the form’s own pass field, which still checks against 0 rather than fewer than 10 (act-pou-form-threshold).

Hygiene promotion and gender

Sessions held at the water points we maintain, who came, and whether each year meets the hygiene-campaign obligation. Managed portfolio only; the figures follow the scope buttons.

The obligation. The registered methodology requires that “The project must conduct annual water hygiene education campaigns for the end-users” (ERSDWS v1.0, parameter SDWS 20, which governs this crediting period), reported each year “in a detailed ‘Report of annual hygiene campaigns results’”. The VPA-DD commits to “at least one education event each year for end-users … Evidence of the events will be including materials used and number of attendees, disaggregated by gender”. Under v2.0 the parameter is SDWS 24, and “The impacts of the campaign shall be assessed using the WHO/UNICEF JMP Core questions for drinking water and hygiene”. A year counts as meeting it here when it has at least one recorded session on a managed point and a survey of managed points’ users that asks the JMP core hygiene questions (handwashing place observed, with water and soap).

Gardien calendars — the days-not-operational record

Pump attendants keep a paper calendar marking the days the pump was not working. Photographed during maintenance visits, those calendars are the only field record of downtime we have.

347 days operational: the registered cap, the carbon basis
Days operational: the carbon basis, and the evidence that stands
347days operational per point-year: the registered cap and the carbon basis. Nothing above it can be claimed without an operation sensor
0.31%operational evidence: human transcription only. Days Adriaan Mol reads X: 46 of 14,865 observed days
0.41%days Dieu Donné Razafimahatratra reads X: 61 of the same 14,865
0.27%days both read X: 40. A sample of 68 calendars (transcription round 1), not the fleet

Days operational stand at the registered 347, and that is the carbon basis. The registered basis holds DOp,y at 347 days: the methodology allows a higher value only on operation-sensor data, and the calendars are a manual log. What the calendars can do is test the condition for keeping 347 — downtime must not exceed 18 days per point-year. The only evidence on that condition is human transcription. In round 1, on 68 calendars and 14,865 observed days, the two human readers marked X on 0.31% and 0.41% of days, and both on 0.27%. That is a sample of transcribed sheets, drawn for the accuracy assessment, and not a fleet figure. The machine reading that used to be stated here is withdrawn. Against the same days the reader detected 0 of the 40 that both humans marked X, so its counts are not evidence of downtime (round 1, diagnosis).

This is the figure to watch, not the 91.6% above. Nine points in ten have been photographed at some time; that is a different and much easier question. Four points in ten have evidence attached to the year being monitored, which is what SDWS 27 actually needs. The metric improved between 2025 and 2026, so the direction is right and the rate is nowhere near enough — at that rate full coverage arrives after the crediting period ends. It is bounded above by the maintenance visit rate, which fell from 100 visits in March to 2 in the latest month on record, because the calendar is only ever photographed during a visit. Active means the point’s first passing SDWS 3 test falls on or before the year end; usable dated evidence means at least one readable sheet whose printed year could be read and which covers part of that year. Same definitions as the SDWS 27 section below.

The gap is recency, not coverage. Nine points in ten have been photographed at some time, which sounds healthy. But 385 — over half the fleet — were last photographed more than six months ago, on top of the 62 never photographed at all, and the most recent ones cluster around a September 2025 round that was never repeated. A calendar photographed a year ago says nothing about days operational in the current monitoring period.

What the registered text actually says about days operational — quoted from the VPA-DD and both methodology versions

Read from the registered VPA-DD and both methodology versions, not from memory. Every quotation below is verbatim; the full extracts, including §3.3.1 and §17.1.1 in full, are in docs/sdws27_basis.md.

SDWS 27 is a monitored parameter, not a fixed ex ante value. Its box sits in VPA-DD section B.7.1, “Data and parameters monitored”, monitoring frequency “Annually”. Its source of data is “During project, this will be determined through either: 1. Measure directly using operation sensor, or 2. Demonstrate from log of operation and maintenance system.” Its applied value is entered as “Estimate: 347 days”, and its QA/QC reads “Values higher than 347 days may only be applied when option 1 is used. 347 days is 95% of days, in line with pump-maintenance in the literature.” ERSDWS v1.0 carries the same two options in the same order of preference and the same 347 condition, and states no default of its own — in v1.0, 347 appears once, as a ceiling.

v2.0 says the same thing more plainly, and names 347 for what it is. Days operational is SDWS 32 in v2.0, not SDWS 31 — SDWS 31 is the premises count. Option 2 there is “Demonstrate from log of operation and maintenance system… detailing uptime and downtime”, and the treatment of uncertainty reads “Values higher than 347 days (95% of days) may only be applied when Option 1 (sensor) is used. Uncertainty is managed by this conservative cap when relying on manual logs.” Downtime is defined in a v1.0 footnote (fn. 13) as “time during which the technology is out of action or unavailable for use”.

So the registered basis is DOp,y = min(DOcap, days demonstrated by the operation-and-maintenance log), with the cap at 347 days, unless an operation sensor is used. The gardien calendars are a manual log. They can confirm the registered 347, and they can oblige us to apply less than 347 where they show more than 18 days of downtime in a year. They cannot raise it. What they show is established by human transcription only: the machine reading that used to be quoted here is withdrawn, because in round 1 it detected none of the days both human readers marked X.

Methodology version — v1.0 governs this crediting period; v2.0 applies at renewal

The VPA is registered under ERSDWS v1.0, and the Design Review assurance form names it throughout as the applied methodology. v2.0 enters into force about 7 October 2026 — §3.3.1: “The date of entry into force is 90 days from the publication date of this methodology” — and §3.3 contains nothing else: no grandfathering clause and no provision for an activity already registered. The only version-transition provision in either document is §17.1.1: “At the renewal, the activity developer shall apply the latest version of this methodology available at the time of submission for renewal”. So v1.0 governs the current crediting period and v2.0 applies at renewal.

Both documents were read end to end. 6 divergences touch what we collect, compute or evidence, and all 6 require action now, each with its own item on the action list. The register is docs/methodology_version_map.md. Eight further differences — parameter renumbering, the §3.4.3 cross-reference error, the cap wording, the market-leakage default, non-eligible uses on piped systems, baseline construction, the eligibility cross-reference and the renewal reassessment list — are methodology interpretation rather than collection, and sit with the Head of Carbon. They were removed from the register on 23 September 2026. In outline:

What that is worth, per year, on the real register §
Withdrawn: the per-year carbon quantification. Its basis is being rebuilt.

This table reported carbon points active and point-years for 2024, 2025 and 2026, and computed every tonnage and USD figure from them. The figures have been removed, not corrected. The basis they rest on — which points were active in which year — does not exist in this repository: there is no commissioning date, no per-point first-rehabilitation set and no per-year activity set, and premiere_rehabilitation.csv is header-only. Nothing here could be recomputed or checked, so nothing here could be shown to a verifier.

They were unreproducible, which is not the same as wrong. No error has been found in any of them; what is missing is the working, and a figure whose working cannot be produced does not belong on a page a verifier reads. They return when the basis is rebuilt under act-carbon-year-basis, which is the one piece of work that restores the whole monetary framing at once.

The carbon denominator used everywhere else on this page is 732, computed from the register every build, and is unaffected.

2024 is zero, and that is not a gap in the data. The VPA-DD sets the start of crediting for each point at its first passing SDWS 3 test — “The crediting for each project water point will begin following a successful SDWS 3 water quality test, demonstrated in the Project Database”. The earliest passing test on the register is 11 April 2025. No point could credit in 2024, so the 93 calendar sheets dated 2024 that the extraction called days on (more 2024 sheets are dated in the coverage table below, which does not need day calls) carry operational information and no carbon value.

The two right-hand columns size the sensor decision. They are not value available to us. The calendars are a manual log, so nothing they show can be applied above the 347-day cap. The tonnage and cash equivalents are withdrawn with the per-year basis.

What the calendars are actually for, stated plainly. Retaining the registered 347 days requires showing that downtime did not exceed 18 days per point-year — a common year less the cap. That is the whole job. The calendars are the operation-and-maintenance log that demonstrates it, point by point and year by year. No calendar-wide reading of that condition is stated: the machine reading is withdrawn, and the human transcription covers a sample of 68 calendars. The risk the calendars carry is downward, not upward: a point whose log showed more than 18 days of downtime would have to be applied at less than 347, and a point with no log at all cannot demonstrate the condition at all. Better calendar evidence protects the registered figure; it cannot increase it.

The number that matters is the other one, and it is far larger. Most of what 2026 carries at 347 days is not yet evidenced by a calendar. The tonnage and cash equivalents are withdrawn with the per-year basis they were computed from. 435 of the 732 carbon points have no dated 2026 sheet at all. A full-year 2026 round recovers evidence for the registered figure; it does not add to it.

The open exposure, stated in points and days

Two questions the documents do not answer decide how much of the claim rests on evidence and how much on the registered estimate alone. Whether the operation-and-maintenance log may be sampled or must cover every point; and what becomes of a point whose calendar is lost or illegible. Neither is settled in either methodology version or in the VPA-DD — the reasoning and the quotations are in docs/sdws27_basis.md.

The exposure used to be stated in tonnes and dollars. Those figures have been withdrawn, because every one of them was computed from the per-year quantification above, whose basis does not exist in this repository. They were unreproducible rather than wrong — no error was found in any of them — and they return when act-carbon-year-basis is closed.

The risk itself is unchanged, and it can be stated in two quantities that do derive. 435 of 732 carbon points have no readable dated 2026 calendar sheet on file. Every one of those points rests on the registered estimate of 347 days operational and has nothing on file to demonstrate it — and 347 is a ceiling a manual log may not exceed, so the evidence can only ever confirm the registered figure, never raise it.

If the log may be sampled and a lost calendar falls back to the registered estimate, that exposure is close to nil. If it must cover every point, those points cannot demonstrate their days operational at all. The honest position is that we do not know which, and the question is first on the action list. The recovery round closes the gap either way, which is why it is worth running before the answer arrives rather than after.

§ Contingent on the SDWS 27 basis being settled — first item on the action list, with the Head of Carbon. Points active in a year are those whose first passing SDWS 3 test falls on or before the year end, pro-rated by the part of the year they were credited; Marolinta is excluded throughout; per-point annual emission reductions are the registered 31.3 tCO2e in Anosy and 27.9 in Maroantsetra, scaling linearly in DOp,y. These per-point registered values are quoted from the registration document and are unaffected by the withdrawal: what was withdrawn is everything computed from the per-year activity basis, which does not exist in this repository.

‡ The accuracy assessment of the machine reading has reported, and the machine reading is withdrawn. In transcription round 1 (two human readers, 68 calendars the machine reads) the reader detected 0 of the 40 days both marked X; see round 1 and the diagnosis. Nothing on this page depends on the machine reading, and DOp,y stands at the registered 347 days.

Where the photographs live. Calendar photographs sit on three mWater questions. Preventive maintenance 2.15.6 is the field of record and carries 1,202; preventive maintenance 2.15.5, the gardiens’ calendar generally, carries 844; repair-after-breakdown 1.3.1.3 carries 321. 2,367 calendar photographs on file in total, 2,348 of them on one of the 736 managed points.

From 20 September 2026 the calendar photograph is mandatory wherever a calendar is present, and absence is recorded rather than inferred. Before the visit ends the technician says whether a calendar is physically on the wall. If it is, the photograph is required. If it is not, no photograph is demanded and the reason is recorded instead — never hung, lost or destroyed, removed by a third party, replaced and taken away, or other. That distinction is the whole point. A photograph field that is mandatory whatever the answer does not produce calendars; it produces something, and 193 of the photographs on file are signboards, pump heads, posters and portraits. A point with no sheet on the wall now says so, on the visit, instead of arriving here months later as a silent gap indistinguishable from a technician who forgot.

The three questions, on both forms — codes, ids and how the condition is enforced

Three questions sit together in group d5233b2b of the preventive-maintenance form, and the same three on repair-after-breakdown. 2.15.5bis asks whether a gardien calendar is physically present at the water point — required, no condition. 2.15.6, the field of record, is required whenever that answer is yes. Where the answer is no, 2.15.5ter takes the reason. Both photograph fields are gated, not just the field of record: 2.15.5 and 2.15.6 on preventive maintenance, 1.3.1.3 on repair after breakdown. Question ids e04e8727… / 27d22a1d… and 1dfdba4b… / 56042233…. The design is snapshotted in data/mwater_form_snapshot.json and the required-when-present condition is asserted on every build, so a later form edit that quietly relaxes it fails the checker. Per-point detail: data/gardien_calendar_coverage.csv, versioned with this report. The two photograph counts differ because 19 calendar photographs sit on water points outside the managed register.

How fresh this is. Every statement on this page about what an mWater form captures or requires is checked against a snapshot of the live form designs, read from mWater on 7 October 2026 — today. 13 forms, 780 questions; preventive-maintenance _rev 505, repair-after-breakdown _rev 393. The snapshot is refreshed as part of the weekly build wherever the network and credentials are available, and the build fails rather than publishes if it is more than 7 days old — so a form changed in the mWater designer cannot sit unnoticed behind a conformance claim for longer than that. Snapshot: data/mwater_form_snapshot.json; statement by statement in docs/sop_form_conformance.md.

The SOP said this field was mandatory for months, and it never was. Chapter 11 of the calendar SOP asserted it; 2.15.6 carried required: false from the day it was written until 20 September. Nothing caught it, because nothing had ever compared a sentence in a procedure with the form it describes. So every current SOP was swept against the live forms to see whether that was one mistake or a pattern. On the day of the sweep, 20 September — the form snapshot below is newer and counts more forms and questions — 15 SOPs, 12 live mWater forms, 748 questions; 233 paragraphs mention a form, field or requirement, 77 make a checkable claim, and 25 resolve to a specific form, field or requirement. Of those 25, 16 conform and 9 do not. Five discrepancies are now closed — the two the SOP itself got wrong, the calendar photograph left unconditionally mandatory on both forms, and every duplicated question code: nine collisions across four forms, all cleared, none remaining. A sixth, meter photographs required on every response where the SOP asks for them only on new or uncalibrated meters, costs technician time and loses no evidence, so it is recorded with no action. Three remain, and they are decisions rather than form edits: an mWater field the decommissioning SOPs rely on that exists on no live form, which is now a paper for Jan; a household-consent field that is optional and holds 0 answers in 142 responses while the protocol makes consent a step; and an SDWS 3 emergency-event form that the SOP names and that, across every form this account can see, paged to exhaustion, does not exist. Statement by statement in docs/sop_form_conformance.md.

The procedure is now one document: SOP-MAD-SDWS27-CalendrierGardien-v1.7-2026 (Water Documents/SOPs/, approved 29 September 2026; earlier versions in SOPs/Archive), which supersedes the calendar provisions previously split between the preventive-maintenance SOP and the water-point removal SOP, and fixes 2.15.6 as the field that carries the evidence. Version 1.3 made a sheet state its own period, and version 1.4 settles how. The year is no longer printed at the press. The template prints none, and carries instead a written year box beside the pump identifier box — outlined the same way, labelled TAONA / ANNÉE, filled in with the pump number when the sheet is hung. The press cannot know which period a sheet will cover, and the measurements say it routinely guesses wrong: of the sheets whose printed year could be read, 29% carry a year already fully elapsed and 17% a year not yet begun, and the forward-dated ones are in service rather than in stock. Where an older sheet carries a printed year, that year denotes the print run and nothing else. Version 1.3 went further than that, and version 1.4 reverses it. To make one blank stock serve any year, v1.3 also made the grid year-agnostic: it dropped the weekday letter and printed February through the 29th on every sheet. The premise was wrong. Identical stock across years was never a requirement — the distribution problem that made the pump number handwritten was 732 point-specific variants, whereas a year is one variant per year and prints as one run. So nothing was gained and two real things were lost: the weekday letter, which is what a gardien uses to find today’s row, and the seventh always-impossible cell. That cell is not cosmetic. A twelve-by-thirty-one grid has seven cells that cannot exist in a common year and six in a leap year, and those cells are the only false-positive probe the extraction has that needs no human transcript. Printing a usable 29 February checkbox on a common-year sheet invited a mark on a day that does not exist and shrank the floor the reader measures itself against. v1.4 takes the year as a parameter and prints a year-correct grid — true month lengths, weekday letters — while printing the year nowhere. The grid may be made for a year; the sheet does not assert one. Where the printed grid and the handwritten box disagree, the box governs, and the reader applies the month lengths of the written year. The corner fiducials, the checkbox grid and the shading are unchanged throughout: every checkbox in Template-v1.1 is at the same coordinate in the 2026 Template-v1.4, and the checker builds a sheet from the controlled generator on every run and counts its impossible cells. Template, generator and SOP all move to v1.4, published for 2026 and 2027; v1.3 is in SOPs/Archive/. Earlier versions remain the record of what they added — the custody rule at v1.2, the header-in-frame requirement at v1.1.

Method — what SDWS 27 requires, how the calendars evidence it, and the machine extraction

This is SDWS 27 evidence. DOp,y is days the project technology is operational for end-users in premises p in year y, and p is the premises type — the same p as SDWS 25 and SDWS 26 — not the water point. The value applied in the VPA-DD is 347 days. Values above 347 may be applied only where an operation sensor is used; operation sensors may themselves be applied on a (90/10) sample basis. 347 days is the default available to any project without sensors — 95% of days — so it is the normal position for a project of this kind, not a shortfall against something better. What has to be demonstrated is that the evidence is representative of the stratum, not complete for every point.

Decided 21 September 2026: the gardien calendar is the official record of days operational, and the call centre is not. The call centre is a dispatch device — an open ticket means the report-back did not arrive, not that the pump is still broken. Where a ticket and a calendar disagree the calendar governs, because SDWS 27 option 2 is “demonstrate from log of operation and maintenance system” and the calendar is that log. No carbon quantity on this page is computed from call-centre data, and the checker fails the build if one appears; the call-centre figures stay under maintenance as an operational signal with no carbon quantity attached. Decision log: docs/decision_log.md. Five open questions on this basis go to Gold Standard together — settle the SDWS 27 basis.

Why DO is indexed on the premises type, quoted from the registered documents

The registered VPA-DD, page 58, sets out Equation 5 with three of its four terms reading “premises type p” in so many words — HHp,y, HNp,y and QPWp — and ERSDWS v1.0 and v2.0 carry the same equation and the same wording. A product summed over one index is only coherent if every factor shares it. The DO box itself says “premises p” and drops the word type the other three carry; read alone it could be taken for an individual premises, read as the fourth factor of that product it cannot. Three things in the registered documents point the same way and none points the other: the VPA-DD applies one value, “Estimate: 347 days”, where a per-pump parameter would need 732; v1.0’s QA/QC limits the days “for schools and other institutions” by the number of school days, a qualification on a category and not on a pump; and the VPA-DD ties the parameter to the maintenance programme as a whole. Quoted in full in docs/sdws27_basis.md. The indexing does not loosen the cap: 347 binds on the method — manual log rather than operation sensor — not on the indexing, and a stratum average above 347 is no more claimable than a per-point one.

Days operational as a stratum average: withdrawn

The stratum averages that stood here were computed from the machine reading and are withdrawn (days operational per point-year by district and sheet year, before and after an error floor measured on impossible cells). The reader they came from detected 0 of 40 days both human readers marked X in round 1. They return only if the reader passes the validation gate (sensitivity of at least 90% and specificity of at least 99% against days both humans mark X); the build fails otherwise. The registered basis holds DO at 347 regardless.

Is the evidenced subset representative?

On the day-call basis, 317 of the 736 points in the managed register on the custody date, 2026-09-19 (745 today; the pump that joined on 23 September is not in the stratum) — 43.1% — have a calendar the extraction can call days on. The test is whether those 317 on the day-call basis differ systematically from the 419 that do not.

The two counts of “points with evidence”, and which question each answers

Two counts are in use on this page and both are correct under their own definition. They are not interchangeable and neither is wrong, so each is named wherever it appears. The day-call basis counts points the extraction produces day calls for, with an observed window of at least 30 days, in any sheet year: 319 points, 317 of them inside the managed register of 736. The 2026-dated-sheet basis counts points holding at least one readable sheet whose year could be read and which covers part of 2026: 299 points among every water point the reader read, 297 of them in the carbon fleet (the count used for the carbon evidence), or 308 if forward-dated sheets were reattributed to the year they were photographed in. The day-call basis is used for anything that reads the marks — the representativeness test below — because a day call is what those need; the 2026-dated-sheet basis is used for coverage of the year being monitored, because that is a question about which period is evidenced and not about how well a sheet was read. The day-call basis is the larger because it spans 2024, 2025 and 2026 sheets; the 2026 basis is narrower in year and wider in what counts as readable.

Yes, it is biased, on one dimension and strongly. District and pump type are close to flat — 43.9% against 40.9%, 42.9% against 44.0% — and neither would trouble a stratum average. Visit frequency is not flat at all: a point with six or more photographs on file is evidenced at 65.8% and a point with one or two at 22.2%, a more than threefold difference. The evidence base is a picture of the well-visited half of the fleet. Points first recorded in 2025 are also over-represented, 55.3% against 39.9%, which is the same effect from another angle. Visit frequency is itself falling — maintenance visit frequency has collapsed.

What the calendars have to carry

The calendars are the evidence for days operational. The gardien calendars are the operation-and-maintenance log, and an annual human-read sample of them is the check on that log; repair and call-centre records are not converted into days (decision 7 Oct 2026). A missing calendar does not void a point’s day count — it weakens the evidence that any downtime was captured. This fits the 347-day default rather than fighting it: 347 is claimed, the calendars show the days deducted, and only an operation sensor could support a figure above it. The 62 points with no calendar photograph and the 385 with nothing current weaken that deduction record.

The worked precedent — how the Improved Cooking VPA evidenced the same parameter

The programme’s first cooking monitoring period was evidenced this way: technology days are computed in the project database and recorded downtime is discounted from them. Its monitoring report states that the database “records information about each technology, such as repairs, replacement, downtime, and number of project technology-days”, and against 13,715,217 technology days it discounted 1,209 days for maintenance and 7,370 for unit transfer — 8,579 days, 0.063% — supported by a spreadsheet of repairs and transfers.

If the stroke loggers are accepted as operation sensors

The metering programme is fleet-wide, not a sample. The StrokeMeter Technical Development Plan v1.2 (18 July 2026, approved-for-execution) sizes a Stroke Logger permanently mounted to every metered pump, and a portable Calibration Pod which the plan is explicit operates as a sampling-campaign instrument and not as a fleet rotation. The plan's unit and fleet counts are not reproduced here: they are illustrative figures written to brief a supplier, and a figure on this page is a form response, a registered parameter or a named decision. The managed fleet is 745. The 90/10 sample establishes litres per counted event. It does not decide which pumps are metered — every pump is. The plan works to the MadAvance census of 17 July 2026; the register has since moved to 745 managed points — brief Curtech on the unit count and the calibration sample.

If the logger is accepted as an operation sensor, this section changes completely. Days operational would come from fleet-wide instrument evidence rather than a manual log; the 347-day cap would cease to bind, because it exists only for the manual-log option — “Values higher than 347 days… may only be applied when Option 1 (sensor) is used.” The gardien calendars would retire as a carbon instrument, remaining the historical record for the periods before metering and an operational tool for the maintenance teams. That is contingent on the definition question and on the programme delivering — put the sensor definition to Gold Standard. Until both land, the calendars are the only days-operational evidence we have.

The plan’s guiding principles, verbatim, and the clause error it carries through

First principle: “Methodology-native: every design decision traces to a clause of SDWS V2.0 — the logger is the SDWS 28 Option 2 operation sensor; the pod is its documented volumetric calibration instrument per §14.4.4; the stroke log doubles as the SDWS 31/32 O&M and days-operational evidence.” Second principle: “Meter every pump, calibrate by sampling: every pump carries a logger and every stroke is counted, but litres-per-counted-event is a FLEET conversion factor per pump type, established on a stratified random sample of pumps and their real users to the GS Sampling Guideline 90/10 bar (90% confidence, ±10% precision of the mean) and re-verified annually on a small sample.” The rationale given is that “delivered volume per stroke is operator-dependent on both pump types… pumps are alike, people differ”, and the logger “maintains a monotonic event counter and per-hour totals in flash”. The plan’s “SDWS 31/32” carries through the cross-reference error in v2.0 §3.4.3 itself, which cites SDWS 31 for the operation-and-maintenance log when SDWS 31 is the premises count and the log belongs to SDWS 32. This was divergence 2 in the version register until 23 September, when it was moved to the eight further differences listed with the register.

The same row finder now decides which sheets get day calls. What it means. The figures above are almost entirely blank days read alike. Transcription round 1 shows the reader does not detect marked days: it detected 0 of the 40 days both human readers marked X (sensitivity 0.0%, specificity 99.6%, κ -0.004 against Adriaan Mol and -0.004 against Dieu Donné, about zero), so its counts are not evidence of downtime. Every machine-derived downtime figure is withdrawn from this page (diagnosis; act-transcription-round, still open).

Why the calendar reader misses marks, and the fix so far

For each of the 40 days both human readers marked X in round 1, and 40 days both read blank (a seeded draw), the reader’s own geometry was re-run on the photograph and the cell it samples saved beside the human mark (crops and measures, tools/diagnose_reader.py). Each X day was then classed by eye:

The threshold alone rules out every X. The reader calls a cell marked when ink covers 0.2 of its window and illegible from 0.12; on the 40 X days the most ink it measured was 0.077, against up to 0.094 on blank days. So even where its window sat on the X it could not call it, and the days it did call marked are not where the humans see marks. The misses fall on 2024, 2025 and 2026 sheets alike (the 2027 sheets have no observed day and are held out), so the template is not the cause; of the 21 sheets in the set that had to be turned for the transcription page, the reader’s own orientation search read all but one.

What v3 changes (tools/caltools.py, read_v3): the grid is registered on the printed text, the month names fixing each column and the day numbers each column’s rows, so a leaning or curled column is followed; ink is measured against the local paper with the printed rules removed, so blue, purple and pencil count; and each cell is compared with what the sheet prints there, its day number and weekday, so only what was written remains. Machine extraction from the calendar photographs — internal only

None of the figures in this block is the figure of record. They come from software that reads the photographs of the gardiens’ calendars and counts the marked days. Every one carries the footnote below, and no published emission-reduction or days-operational figure of record derives from these files — DOp,y stands exactly where it did.

516pump-periods with day calls †
362water points †
131,129day cells actually observed †
90,884grid cells the day had not reached, counted per image †
0.28median confidence, a score between zero and one †

Two gates, two questions. Whether a sheet can be read at all is decided by fitting twelve month columns to the printed rules; whether individual days can be called on it is decided separately, by registering the day rows to the same rules. 1,413 photographs pass the first, 608 the second. Coverage figures use the first; every day-level figure uses only the second.

Machine-read downtime: withdrawn. In transcription round 1 the reader detected 0 of the 40 days both human readers marked X (sensitivity 0.0%, specificity 99.6%), so the days it calls marked are not evidence of downtime. No figure computed from its marks — a marked rate, an error floor, a count of days not operational or an uptime — is shown on this page, and the build fails if one is while data/reader_validation.json does not show the reader validated. Even a validated reading is not a figure we can apply above the cap: the calendars are a manual log, and the registered basis holds days operational at 347. Transcription check, round 1; why the reader misses.

How the cells are classified

What a calendar photograph can and cannot show. A sheet photographed on a given date carries marks only for the days up to that date. Every later cell is blank because the day had not arrived, not because the pump was working. Each printed cell is therefore classified three ways from the year printed on the sheet itself and the date of the photograph: observed, not yet observed, or not a date at all. Every rate is computed over observed cells only. A 2024 sheet photographed in a later year is fully observed, while a 2027 sheet photographed in 2026 shows nothing at all.

Days that cannot exist. Every sheet prints a twelve-by-thirty-one grid, so in a common year seven of its cells are days that cannot exist — 29, 30 and 31 February, and 31 April, June, September and November — and in a leap year six: 4,163 such cells on the sheets with day calls. They are not days, and no figure counts them.

“Could not be read” and “had not happened yet” are different states. These are counted per pump-period — one per point-year, 516 of them, several photographs of the same sheet year merged — so they are smaller than the per-image cell counts above. On observed cells the software calls 1,352 days illegible †. Separately, 77,324 cells lay beyond the photograph date and were never evidence of anything; of those the software called 2,734 illegible. The two are counted separately everywhere and are never added together.

Source files: data/calendar_extraction_summary.csv, data/calendar_extraction_figures.json, data/calendar_not_calendar.csv and data/calendar_year_coverage.csv, all regenerated by recompute_figures.py and coverage.py from the reader output.

The year has to be read off the sheet, and on 399 readable photographs it cannot be. Of 1,413 readable photographs the printed year could be read on 1,014. Sheets whose year could not be read are excluded from every rate rather than assigned a year — an undated sheet cannot be attached to a monitoring year, so it evidences nothing however well it is read. The 608 of them the extraction can also call days on — the basis of every day-level figure on this page, not all the dated sheets — are, by year: 93 for 2024, 199 for 2025, 239 for 2026, 77 for 2027. Quantify the water points behind the undatable sheets.

What the year printed on a sheet denotes, and why the photograph date cannot stand in for it

Among the 749 sheets dated by the first year-reading pass (19 September; the later reader run behind the rest of this section dates 1,014, and the coverage table below counts 152 sheets printed 2027 on that basis, which it shows as 133 point-years), 54% carry the year they were photographed in, 29% an earlier year and 17% a later one, so the photograph date is not a safe substitute. A printed year later than the photograph does not mean an unused sheet. In that first pass 117 sheets carry a printed 2027 and were photographed during 2026. The printed year is real: under magnification a sample of them shows a crisp, unambiguous 2027, and none a different year; the OCR string is literally paompy 2027 ID, and confidence runs 0.8 to 1. Whether those sheets were in use when they were photographed cannot be read from the machine’s marks, which are withdrawn; it is part of the question open as act-printed-year-meaning.

What the printed year records is the sheet’s edition or print run, not reliably the period it covers — and the template no longer prints one: from Template-v1.3 onward the year is written on the sheet by the technician who hangs it, Template-v1.4 is the current issue, and on older stock a printed year denotes the print run only. The consequence for coverage is bounded and small: attributing those sheets to the photograph’s year instead would move water points with 2026 evidence — the 2026-dated-sheet basis, every water point the reader read, 297 of them in the carbon fleet — from 299 to 308, because most of the 107 points affected already hold another 2026 sheet. The figures here stay on the printed-year basis, which is the conservative one. Establish what the printed year is meant to denote. 93 sheets are 2024, a leap year: on those, 29 February is a real day.

193 of the photographs are not calendars. Every calendar photograph on file was inspected by eye. 33 of them the reader had accepted as calendars and they are excluded from every figure here; 160 it had already thrown out. A person holding up a calendar is counted as a calendar, however badly framed. A second look on 6 October 2026 found 13 of the photographs first flagged to be real calendars after all; they are marked as such in data/calendar_not_calendar.csv and count in every calendar figure again. The rest are listed there with water point, question and reason, and stay where they are in mWater by decision of 6 October 2026: the report excludes them using that reviewed list, and the cause is addressed instead, with hints on the calendar photograph questions and a briefing of the field teams — brief the teams on the calendar photograph.

What the 193 non-calendar photographs are, and which question they sit on

70 of the blue “Point d’Eau Potable et Pérenne” signboard, 66 of a printed document other than a calendar, 17 of a standpipe or pump head, 39 portraits or site views with no sheet in the frame, and 1 of a sample bottle on a pump platform. By question: 109 on 2.15.5, 72 on 2.15.6, 12 on 1.3.1.3.

One pump-period had been lost to the exclusion and is restored: water point 742896406, 2025 holds a signboard and a usable calendar, and the signboard had been selected. The selection is now re-run after exclusion rather than rows being deleted. Three pump-periods held a non-calendar alongside a usable image and no other point was affected; five pump-periods whose only day-call image was a non-calendar are correctly gone.

What an operation sensor would size, and nothing else. None of this is available on calendar evidence — the methodology permits a value above 347 days only on measured sensor data — for this programme the StrokeMeter — so the arithmetic exists to size the instrumentation decision and for no other purpose. Emission reductions are 27.9 tCO2e per community water supply per year in the VPA-DD at 347 days, and DOp,y enters the volume calculation linearly. The span from 347 days to a full common year is +5.19%, or +1.51 tCO2e per point per year on the Maroantsetra figure with its fNRB applied at 36%. Fort-Dauphin carries the higher baseline emission factor (0.00027 against 0.00018 tCO2e/L as registered), so that span is wider there. With the Maroantsetra fNRB applied at 36% rather than the registered 34% (both MoFuSS-derived; James Walker, 21 Sep 2026), its emission factor becomes 0.000189 tCO2e/L and its emission reductions 29.2 tCO2e per community water supply per year, from the registered 27.9. A sensor would not deliver a full year either: it would deliver whatever it measures, and the metering programme is fleet-wide — a logger on every metered pump — so the comparison is the whole programme against the whole fleet, not a per-unit trade. Whether it is worth the instrumentation is a decision for the Head of Carbon, not a conclusion of this page.

How much of a year the calendars actually evidence

This is the binding constraint, and it is not about how well the sheets are read. A calendar evidences a year only up to the day it was photographed; where a point has several photographs of the same year, the latest governs and the earlier ones corroborate it. Across 795 point-years with a readable, dated sheet, the median share of the year carrying photographic evidence is 58%, and 496 of them have less than 90% of the year covered.
