What that means for SDWS 27. A year that is already over can be evidenced end to end, because the sheet was photographed after it closed. The year being monitored cannot be, because the photograph is taken during it. So the calendars cannot carry a full-year days-operational figure for the current period however well they are read — which is the cooking precedent reached from the other direction: technology days are computed for the estate, and the calendars discount recorded downtime within the stretches they actually cover. Per-point detail: data/calendar_year_coverage.csv.

Coverage, after recalibrating the reader. Four template generations are in the field — 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 — and the reader now fits a twelve-column grid to the rules actually printed on the sheet instead of assuming one generation’s spacing. Of 2,364 calendar photographs in the image backup the reader works from (2,367 are on file in mWater; 3 of them are missing from the backup and were never read), 33 are not calendars and are excluded; of the remainder it reads 1,413, against 1,156 on the first reader, and can call individual days on 608. At the level that matters — visits left with no usable image — of 966 visits that produced a calendar photograph, 805 (83.3%) carry at least one readable image and 161 (16.7%) carry none, against 217 on the first reader. At water-point level, 83 points have never produced a usable calendar image, against 110 on the first reader.

The reissue list needs two different instructions, not one. Of those 83 points, 38 have never had a calendar photographed at all — every image on the record is a signboard, a pump, a poster or a portrait — 18 have a mixture, and only 27 have a calendar photograph the reader genuinely could not read. Telling the first 38 that their photograph was unreadable would send the field team to fix the wrong thing. data/calendar_no_usable_image.csv carries the cause and the field action for each: 75 in Maroantsetra, 8 in Fort-Dauphin, and only 4 where the portrait field is the sole source. These 83 are not the 62 counted above: those have no calendar photograph at all, out of 736 managed points; the 83 have photographs of which none is readable, out of the 681 water points that have any — every point the photographs name, managed or not; of the managed points, 674 have one. A point can be in both sets. Run the 2026 calendar recovery round.

How the accuracy assessment is being made

The sample basis. 50 calendars sit inside the frame and are the set on which a human can be compared with a machine: 17 kept from the original draw and 33 drawn since to bring the round up to size. That satisfies the minimum under either methodology version — the Clean Development Mechanism floor of 30 for a proportion parameter carried into ERSDWS v1.0 §4.2.2, and the 50 per sample group or stratum required by v2.0 §14.5.3 — so the assessment stands whichever version governs, and will not need repeating at renewal. The draw is stratified by district (36 Maroantsetra, 14 Fort-Dauphin) and across the full quality range (10 in quartile 1, 14 in quartile 2, 13 in quartile 3, 13 in quartile 4), so it is not a sample of easy sheets. A further 33 sheets stay in the round outside the frame, where the machine produced nothing: they are scored human against human only and are never folded into the machine figure. Re-scope every sample against the v2.0 minimum of 50.

What any agreement figure will and will not cover. An agreement figure from this round applies to the photographs the extraction produces output for — currently 608 of 1,413 readable calendar photographs and 2,367 on file in mWater. It is not a measure of how well the calendars are read; it is a measure of how well the ones the software can read and date are read. That sentence travels with the number — it is printed above the comparison table, written into the head of the comparison output file, and asserted on this page, so an agreement figure can never appear here without it.

The frame, the transcriber’s prior exposure, and why agreement is reported per calendar

The validation frame was corrected on 2026-09-20. The original fifty calendars were drawn from “readable calendar photographs”, which was the wrong population: a human transcript can only be compared with a machine one where the machine produced something to compare, and on the observed-cell basis that also requires a year, because without a year there is no observable window and no month lengths. The frame is now: photographs the extraction produces day calls for, whose year could be read off the sheet, and which are calendars — 608 images. Frame, reason, date and seed are recorded per row in transcription/validation_selection.csv; the draw used seeds 20260920, 20260921, 20260922, and every row records which pass drew it, so the whole selection can be repeated.

The reference transcription is made by Adriaan Mol, from the photographs. That transcriber had already seen the extraction’s aggregate error statistics — the impossible-cell rate, the marked rate, the confidence distribution — though no per-cell output for any sheet, and the page shows none. Prior knowledge of the aggregates is a weaker exposure than seeing the machine’s answers, but it is not zero, and a verifier is entitled to know it before reading the agreement figure. A second transcriber with no such exposure would settle it; the page records who transcribed each sheet so the two can be compared separately.

The cell is not the unit that carries the variation — the calendar is. Cells within one sheet share its paper, its light, its handwriting and its template generation, so agreement must be reported per calendar and aggregated across calendars, not pooled cell-by-cell. The transcription grid locks every cell the photograph could not show, so the human and the machine are compared on exactly the same cells and no one spends time on a cell that was blank by construction.

Transcription page: sanitap-water.github.io/sanitap-water-report/transcription/. It shows the photographs and nothing else — no machine output, no aggregate, no hint of either. Results are not in this report yet. When the transcription round is complete, per-calendar agreement will be added here.

† Machine-extracted from photographs of the gardiens’ calendars. Subject to an accuracy assessment in progress against independent human transcription of 50 calendars. Not the figure of record for SDWS 27 and not used in any emission reduction calculation.

Emission reductions — what the programme is for

The rest of this page explains how many people get safe water. This is what that converts into, how the calculation is built, and how much of it is actually evidenced today.

ex ante indicative

The equation, from the Gold Standard methodology.

BEy = EFb × (1 − Cb − Xcleanboil,y) × Qy × Mq,y
Qy = min(Qm,y , Qpop,y)

Baseline emissions are the fuel that would have been burned boiling water, reduced by the households already drinking safe water, reduced again by those still boiling despite the project, multiplied by the volume actually delivered and by the share of samples meeting the quality standard. Qy takes the lower of measured volume and population-derived volume — you cannot claim more water than you delivered, nor more than the population could drink.

Because Qm,y and DOp,y are not yet evidenced, any emission reduction figure produced from this equation today is an ex ante indicative estimate, not a claim. It cannot be verified as it stands, and no number is presented here as though it could be. Two inputs out of eight are missing, and they are the two that convert people reached into volume delivered — which is the quantity the credits are actually made of. Two more are only partly evidenced: Mq,y until James Walker rules on the 2025 household round, and Xcleanboil,y, which rests on the registered value until it is measured. Cb also rests on its value from validation, which is what the methodology asks of it until it is re-measured. Until the stroke test has run and the calendars are current, the honest output of this page is the method and the evidence status, not a tonnage.

What would change that. The stroke test (SDWS 23) and the calendar recovery round (SDWS 27) are both on the one list with owners and proposed dates. When both land, the two missing inputs are evidenced; the table has eight green rows only once the household-round rulings are in and Xcleanboil,y and Cb are measured, and then the equation produces a figure a verifier can test. Equation and parameter definitions: Gold Standard ERSDWS. Selection reasoning and the confirmation that the five-minute stroke test is the accepted basis: James Walker, Head of Carbon, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 18 September 2026.

The stroke test — how monitored volume gets measured

Parameter SDWS 23 needs a measured volume of water delivered. Until the StrokeMeter is deployed, a timed five-minute pumping test is how a hand pump’s volume is established in the field. The procedure is written and approved at v2.0; it has not been performed on a single pump. So there is no measured volume for any point, SDWS 23 is undetermined, and nothing on this page converts people served into litres delivered. Two questions on this SOP are unresolved; they are in the table below and on the one list.

written, never run
The method, the SOP, and the two open questions on it

The method, in short. The pump rests at least 10 minutes. One technician works the lever at a constant 40 strokes per minute set by a metronome (38–42 accepted; more than 2 strokes per minute off and the test is void) while another times it and never lets the pumper see the clock. Flow is stabilised until two consecutive 10 litre measurements agree within 3%, then the main test runs for five minutes exactly. Two flow rates are computed — the five-minute mean Q_moy and the rate over the last two minutes Q_2der — and the lower of the two is taken as the proxy: qi = min(Q_moy, Q_2der). Taking the lower is the conservative choice, because a pump that fades under sustained use should be credited at the rate it sustains.

Everything else is in the procedure, not here. Roles, pump-specific handling, the mWater form, the invalidity rules and the estimation maths are in SOP-MAD-SDWS27-StrokeTest-v2.0-2026 (April 2026, version 2.0 revised). Do not work from this summary in the field — work from the SOP.

The five-minute test is the accepted basis pending the StrokeMeter. Source: James Walker, Head of Carbon, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 18 September 2026.

Two questions about this SOP, answered by James Walker on 21 Sep 2026
Open questionWhat it turns onResolving
1. Does the quarterly calibration requirement stand? The SOP requires the stroke-count proxy to be calibrated quarterly against direct volumetric measurement, to R² ≥ 0.80 with a regression slope between 0.9 and 1.1, on a minimum of 30 pumps per zone.Answer: the quarterly validation attaches to the Option 3 proxy only, and Gold Standard is expected to withdraw it — the paragraph was published in error — though that will not be confirmed until later this year (watched in the action list). Had it stood, it would have cost a calibration of 30 pumps in each zone every quarter across Maroantsetra and Fort-Dauphin — on top of the test itself, indefinitely. The StrokeMeter annual re-verification stands. The draft stroke-test SOP v2.2 (unsigned, filed beside v2.1) plans on that basis: calibration is re-verified annually, on 50 pump calibrations a year — each a timed 5-minute discharge test against the meter installed on the pump — carried out with a small set of about 5 portable calibration pods, one of them a spare, moved from pump to pump. Those calibrations are separate from the permanently installed stroke meters: at least 100, 50 per stratum.James Walker, 21 Sep 2026; Gold Standard’s confirmation watched
in the action list
2. Which parameter is the stroke test: SDWS 28. The v2.0 stroke-test parameter is SDWS 28 — Option 3, the published ID. The SOP up to v2.1 cited it as SDWS 27 — Option 3, the ID in the consultation version.A numbering discrepancy between our own written procedure and the methodology reference, now settled: SDWS 28 is the published ID of the v2.0 stroke-test parameter; SDWS 27 was its ID in the consultation version. It agrees with the v2.0 box itself: SDWS 28 Option 3 is the box that names standardised stroke tests — quoted in full at reconcile the stroke-test SOP with v2.0. The draft SOP v2.2 cites SDWS 28 throughout. Which version governs this VPA is a separate question.James Walker, 21 Sep 2026

Neither of these is a caveat. Each is a question with an owner and a consequence, and each is answerable. Three further items on this SOP are open: run the test on the SDWS 23 sample, move the SOP into the SOPs folder and sign it off, and reconcile it with v2.0.

Pre-project eligibility: non-functional or non-potable before the project

Methodology 2.2.1(d) and SDWS 12: a point may count only if it was out of order, or its water was not safe, before the project. A rehabilitated hand pump must have been out of order, with no planned maintenance, for at least three months beforehand; a piped system must show water that failed the health-based rule before its works were complete. Every row links to its mWater record so a verifier can open it.

Hand pumps — out of order for three months before the works (2.2.1(d))

728 of the 745 managed pumps in this scope carry the control answered Yes on their first-rehabilitation record and pass the gate: 693 Yes, with photographs and 35 Yes, no photo. A Yes without a photograph counts as eligibility evidence (decision of Adriaan Mol, 4 Oct 2026); those pumps are kept apart as their own status so a verifier can see them. 2 answered No, 1 left it blank, 1 have no first-rehabilitation record, and 13 are Marolinta works on the borehole-progress form, which carries no such control.

The gaps: the 8 records already flagged under 2.2.1(d) — 3 answered No, 5 left blank; 3 of the pumps are in the managed fleet. This is an eligibility question, not a data error: nothing here says the rehabilitation did not happen. The action that closes them.

Piped systems — non-potable before the works (SDWS 12)

A piped system shows it was non-potable before the project when at least one pre-project result fails the health-based rule, E. coli above 0 per 100 ml. A result is pre-project if it is dated before the tap-level protocol went live (22 Sep 2026 15:58 UTC), or before the system’s works completion where that date is recorded. 1 of the 25 systems show it; 24 have no pre-project test.

The baseline must be taken before works completion. Once a system’s works are complete, no test can show its starting situation any more, so a system with no pre-project test cannot show eligibility this way after the event. For Ambohibola, Amboanjo and Andilanatoby the baseline is still possible: take it before their works are completed.

Amboasary gara’s results are pre-project evidence of need. They record the starting situation that qualifies the system for the programme, while its upgrade is under way. They are not a failure or a risk of a managed system, and they call for no corrective action: the system joins the managed portfolio only after its works are complete and its post-works tests are done (the retest at the taps).

Listed exceptions: what may stand in the figures without eligibility evidence

The build fails if a point or system is in the managed or carbon figures with neither eligibility evidence nor an entry here (data/eligibility_exceptions.json) or in the 2.2.1(d) gaps above.

  • 782134540 (managed and carbon): No first-rehabilitation record of any kind: the one recorded exception to the fleet-entry rule (29 Sep 2026), kept on its repair, water-quality and call-centre records until 31 Oct 2026 (data/register_corrections.json). act-782134540-rehab-record.
  • Marolinta (managed only - outside the carbon portfolio): Marolinta works (new boreholes and rehabilitations) are recorded on the borehole-progress form, which carries no 2.2.1(d) control. Separately funded (Deichmann) and outside the carbon portfolio; the exception does not reach any carbon figure.
  • 1125843376, the managed Antananarivo smart-tap kiosk (water point 1125843383) (managed): Commissioned 14 Sep 2026 with no pre-project water quality test; admitted by Adriaan's decision of 25 Sep 2026; post-works test tracked under act-enduro-onboard-6-kiosk-wq.

Register corrections and exclusions

Nothing is deleted in mWater. Where a record and the evidence disagree, the correction is recorded here with the evidence that settled it, and the report is built from the corrected position. A water point excluded here cannot reappear in the portfolio without an entry being removed from this list.

How this is worked out: points with no district in mWater

mWater assigns a water point’s district itself, from its GPS position, against its own map of administrative boundaries; the district cannot be typed in. A few pumps on the shore stand just outside that map, so mWater leaves their district blank. We assign the district from the nearest boundary and the neighbouring points, record the reason against each one, and never move a GPS position to make the map fit.

The carbon calculation — open this for the Gold Standard file

Collapsed because most readers do not need it. Inside: how the credits are calculated, what the cookstove overlap does to the baseline, and every data gap still blocking issuance. Owners and dates are in Open actions below.

SDWS 26 — premises served, from the November 2025 round

The annual monitoring survey asks how often a household draws drinking water from the project water point, once for the dry season and once for the rainy season. A premises counts as served in a season when it reports use at least every two days, and the served share is the average of the dry-season and rainy-season shares. Every figure below expands to its population, rule, form and arithmetic.

Source
SDWS26 on this page, recomputed each run by tools/rebuild_sdws26.py from the annual monitoring survey, form 2eeb8682… (cbn_gender.json), questions WS1.18 (dry season) and WS1.39 (rainy season).
Extracted
Survey pulled 2026-10-07.
Rows
Responses that answered both usage questions, by project scenario (deployment). Part-entries that answered neither are excluded, as stated in the section.
Columns
Served, per season: responses whose answer is every day, more than once a day or every two days, by choice id. Served share: the average of the dry-season and rainy-season shares (James Walker, 23 September 2026). Clusters: communes reached against the VPA-DD B.7.3 minimum. Mean household size: question WS1.12.

The headline is the seasonal average: 99.6% across both scenarios, 99.5% in Fort-Dauphin and 99.8% in Maroantsetra. The both-scenarios figure pools the responses of the two scenarios. Open any average for its working, which also shows the both-seasons and either-season readings as a sensitivity.

The seasonal rule. The served share is the average of two shares: the premises served in the dry season (WS1.18) and the premises served in the rainy season (WS1.39), each over the premises that answered both questions. It is not the share served in both seasons. The served set is Every day, More than 1 time per day and Every 2 days, matched by choice id (J1qZUqA, 6wqmK16, h4uZZBz), never by position: the declared scale is not monotonic, because “more than once a day” sits second. Source for both: James Walker, Carbon Lead, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 23 September 2026 — “Let’s average it to prevent unnecessarily losing credits” on the seasonal rule, and “Correct” on the served set. Recorded in docs/decision_log.md.

What this round does not evidence
  • It evidences the 2025 monitoring period, not 2026. Every response was submitted between 11 November 2025 and 21 November 2025. A 2026 figure needs its own round; this one cannot be carried forward.
  • Maroantsetra reached 6 clusters against the VPA-DD B.7.3 minimum of 8, short by 2. Fort-Dauphin reached 8 and met it. The shortfall is stated rather than rounded away, because a verifier will count the communes.
  • No response carries an approval. All 414 sit unapproved in mWater — act-sdws26-approve-2025.
  • 4 responses are excluded from the denominator as abandoned part-entries: they answered neither usage question, and between 2 and 21 of the form's questions. Counting a part-entry as a non-response understates the proportion; counting it as served overstates it. The exclusion is a stated rule, not a silent filter.

SDWS 25, in passing. Mean household size in this round is 4.47 in Fort-Dauphin and 3.66 in Maroantsetra, which still round to the registered 4.5 and 3.7. Derived from the same round, question WS1.12; the registered values are unchanged and nothing here restates them. The survey form.

Data the carbon programme needs from us

One row for every parameter the methodology requires us to evidence. This report does not run the carbon programme — methodology interpretation, the design review and the Gold Standard relationship are the Head of Carbon's. Where the two meet there is one question, and this is it: can we supply the data, and if not, what is missing and who owns it. Coverage and freshness are computed every build from the populations and the extract manifest; nothing in this table is typed. A new requirement is a row in data/carbon_parameters.json, not a rebuild of this section.

Cookstoves and water: the overlap, measured

Where the two carbon programmes meet the same household. Measured from mWater on 18 September 2026 and checked against the portfolio on 22 September, not modelled. Source: claude/suppressed-demand-baseline-and-the-stove-overlap-2026-09-18.md.

all of Fort-Dauphin, as measured

The overlap is all of Fort-Dauphin, not a fraction of a district. On 22 September all 127 Fort-Dauphin points in the carbon portfolio shared an administrative region with a cookstove distribution. The Fort-Dauphin point that joined on 23 September has not yet been checked against the distribution. Every one lies between latitude −25.18 and −24.25, entirely within Anosy. Maroantsetra is zero. So this is not a scattered 17% of the portfolio; it is one site, completely covered, and that site is 32.7% of the carbon portfolio (Maroantsetra and Fort-Dauphin) by people served — 40,639 of 124,356.

How it was measured. Cookstove distribution form f1fcf0c427ea46d2a702757bece97b39; the household link is the SiteQuestion carrying the household code, joined to entities.household.code, then joined to the water point register on admin_region ids. The join is on ids and not on place names: the two registers spell the same places differently, and a name join silently drops or invents matches.

The risk is not double counting of tonnes. Our baseline is suppressed demand — methodology s3.4.2 credits users drinking unsafe water as if they would have boiled it. Nobody is claiming the same fuel twice. The question is narrower and sharper: what would they have boiled on? SDWS 11 registers the baseline boiling efficiency at 10%, which is a three-stone fire. For a household that holds one of our own improved stoves, the counterfactual device is arguably that stove — and if the baseline device is more efficient, baseline emissions fall in proportion. The exposure is to the efficiency assumption, not to the tonnage arithmetic.

Our own design document already concedes the point. For Anosy it states that "the presence of improved stoves will be reflected in the emission reduction calculations". That commitment is applied, by method: the ex post figures adjust the baseline boiling efficiency by the share of end users who report using an improved cookstove in the annual monitoring.

Registered against monitored. At validation the VPA-DD registered improved cookstoves at 0.4% of premises in Anosy (SDWS 6, p.69). The 2025 annual monitoring found 81% of answering Fort-Dauphin households using one (169 of 208, dry season), and it is the monitored share that adjusts the baseline in the ex post figures. James Walker, Carbon Lead, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 18 Sep 2026: “we adjust in the ex post figures based on the proportion of end users who respond in the annual monitoring that they use an ICS. 2025 in FD had 81%.” The methodology provides for cookstove and safe-water cross-effects, and the stacking prohibition applies to Impact Statements only, not to credits (same email).

The upside and the exposure are the same 128 pumps. Fort-Dauphin sits in Toliary, which carries the sub-national uplift in the fraction of non-renewable biomass (fNRB) — 0.54 against the national 0.36 (see below). The same points that are exposed to the stove-efficiency question are the ones that gain most from the regional fNRB. They must move together: claiming the Toliary uplift while ignoring the stove overlap on the identical set of pumps is the version of this a verifier will not accept.

Parameter SDWS 21 — the fraction of non-renewable biomass, and why it is what it is
Parameter SDWS 21 — fraction of non-renewable biomass (fNRB)

The fraction of non-renewable biomass (fNRB) is the share of firewood displaced by safe water that would not have grown back. It is what prices the baseline.

The applied basis is MoFuSS, under the Gold Standard rule update. The registered parameter is SDWS 21, and the VPA-DD gives its Source of data as MoFuSS, applied “in line with GS Rule Update: fNRB Application for GS4GG Certification V1.0”. That rule update, version 1.0 of 24 April 2025, provides at §2.3.1: “For the issuance of GSVERs, design certification or inclusion of an activity, or renewal of crediting period of a design certified activity, the project developer shall use one of these fNRB values: a. Modelling Fuelwood Saving Scenario (MoFuSS) derived values…” The values are taken under option (a); the rule update is held in Water Documents/Methodology of record/ with its checksum.

A6.4-AMT-009 is not the basis and is no longer cited as one. The rule update’s eligible methods are MoFuSS-derived values, an updated Tool 33 at version 2.0 or later, or a new method developed under PACM-A6.4 and approved by Gold Standard. It does not name A6.4-AMT-009, and the registered values come from MoFuSS, so the tool is not carried here even as a supporting reference. An earlier edition applied 36% to Maroantsetra on an A6.4-AMT-009 sub-national reading; the registered figure is 34%.

What is applied. Maroantsetra is registered at 34% (the MoFuSS value for that region, VPA-DD SDWS 21, p.76) and applied at 36%, the sub-national value, in line with the sub-national value applied for Fort-Dauphin; the correction is made at verification. James Walker, Carbon Lead, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 21 Sep 2026: “It should be 36, so it is inline with what we have applied for FD (sub national rather than commune). I will update that in the verification as a ‘correction’.” The same 36% is the figure James Walker calls the national value when proposing it for the piped VPA (18 September, on the action list); “sub national” here means above commune level, not a different number. Fort-Dauphin 54% is the Toliary provincial figure, because in the VPA-DD’s own words “The project area of Maroantsetra is defined as a region on MoFuSS. The Anosy Region does not have a figure prescribed by MoFuSS. The most relevant figure to apply is the regional figure for Toliary Province, Madagascar. The Provincial figure has been applied due to the nature of wood collection and charcoal production, which crosses district boundaries.”

Stated plainly: this is justifiable, but it is not the most conservative selection available. The portfolio-weighted figure is 0.419 against the national default of 0.36 — a 16.3% uplift, driven entirely by Fort-Dauphin sitting in Toliary. The footnote supports the choice; it does not compel it. A verifier is entitled to ask why the narrower option was taken where it raises the claim, and the answer must be the fuel characteristics, not the outcome.

District values exist but are not applied. The Model for fuelwood savings scenarios (MoFuSS) generates these figures and publishes them at district level: Taolagnaro 32%, Maroantsetra 34%, Moramanga 37%, Toamasina 36%, Antananarivo renivohitra 0%. Maroantsetra’s registered value is 34%; since James Walker’s answer of 21 September the page applies 36%, in line with the sub-national value used for Fort-Dauphin. The others are recorded as available and not used. The district figure for Taolagnaro (32%) is lower than the Toliary provincial value applied to Fort-Dauphin (54%) — the one place a narrower MoFuSS figure exists and is not taken, on the VPA-DD’s reasoning that wood collection and charcoal production cross district boundaries there.

Piped systems are a separate voluntary project activity (VPA). Across it the national 36% is applied rather than the Antananarivo sub-national 26%.

The CDM tools, for the record. CDM TOOL33 “Default values for common parameters” is an alternative eligible method under §2.3.1(b) of the rule update, and only at version 2.0 or later since “version 2.0 or earlier versions are not valid any more”, but it is not the applied basis and is no longer cited as one here. CDM TOOL30 “Calculation of the fraction of non-renewable biomass” was discontinued with effect from 1 January 2026 by decision of the CDM Executive Board at EB 125, which reads “To discontinue TOOL 30 with effect from 1 Jan 2026”. It is not a live source.

Source of the selection reasoning: James Walker, Head of Carbon, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 18 September 2026. The parameter values themselves are the registered SDWS 21 values from MoFuSS as cited above; this email is the source for how the provincial figure was selected for Anosy, not for the numbers.

Stacking — whether an ICS project and a water project may both claim the same household
Stacking — whether an ICS project and a water project may both claim

The question. Gold Standard prohibits stacking under a suppressed demand baseline. Fort-Dauphin has both an improved cookstove (ICS) project and this safe drinking water project. Does the prohibition bite?

The answer: no, not on these credits. The prohibition applies to Certified Impact Statements and Certified Impact Products — it does not apply to verified emission reductions, which is what this programme issues.

The reasoning. The Gold Standard safe drinking water methodology, Emission Reductions from Safe Drinking Water Supply (ERSDWS), expressly provides for cross-effects in both V1 and V2 where an ICS activity and a safe drinking water activity overlap. Gold Standard applies lex specialis — where a specific rule and a general rule both cover the same facts, the specific rule governs. The cross-effect provisions in ERSDWS are the specific rule; the general stacking prohibition is the general one.

Recorded equally plainly: this has been applied successfully but never challenged. It has passed validation and verification in practice, and no VVB has yet tested it. Precedent is not enforceable. A future VVB is entitled to reach a different view, and nothing in the file compels it not to. This is a reasoned position, not a settled one.

Source: James Walker, Head of Carbon, email “Re: Water program dashboard & actions”, 18 September 2026.

Carbon data gaps — the list Jan drives

Everything still to be gathered before issuance, ranked by what blocks it. One list, one owner each, reported to the SLT weekly. Source: claude/carbon-data-gaps-what-we-still-must-gather-2026-09-18.md.

9 gaps

The cookstove overlap is measured — all of Fort-Dauphin, set out below. What is missing is not the arithmetic but the instrument: nobody has asked which stove a household uses to boil water. It is a measurement gap, not a calculation gap, and it is listed below as such. The source document still opens by saying the overlap has not been calculated — correcting it is on the action list.

GapWhat it blocksOwner
1. Baseline boiling device where a household holds one of our stoves. The overlap itself is measured — all 127 Fort-Dauphin points in the portfolio on 22 September (one has joined since, not yet checked), 32.7% of people served in the carbon portfolio. What is unresolved is SDWS 11: the baseline efficiency is registered at 10%, a three-stone fire, and for a stove-holding household the counterfactual device is arguably the improved stove. Decide the treatment and implement the design document’s own commitment that “the presence of improved stoves will be reflected in the emission reduction calculations”.Blocks issuance — the first thing a VVB will test on Fort-DauphinJames Walker on method, Adriaan on data
2. Renewal dates for SDWS 6, 8, 11, 12. Set at validation, untracked since, renewal frequency not yet read out of the methodology.Blocks issuance — an expired baseline parameter invalidates the emission factorJames Walker
3. SDWS 23 continuous monitoring. One smart meter is live on an Endur’O urban system. The hand-pump fleet has no monitored volume at all; the stroke meter needs a litres-per-stroke constant, and even calibrated it is not continuous monitoring.Blocks issuance — Method 1 cannot close without itAdriaan / MadAvance
4. SDWS 27 days operational. 62 points have never had a gardien calendar photographed; 385 more were last photographed over 6 months ago (calendar custody as at 2026-09-19). The O&M-log route carries a 347-day ceiling in any case; without the log we cannot evidence days operational at all.Caps the claimAngelo and Jan
5. SDWS 26 usage survey. Measured for 2025 from the November 2025 round — served share 99.6%. Each monitoring period needs its own round, at least 100 households per scenario at 90% confidence and a 10% margin of error, and Maroantsetra must reach the cluster minimum.Caps the claim — each period’s premises cannot be counted as served without its own roundAdriaan / MadAvance
6. SDWS 25 people per premises. INSTAT RGPH-3 is the source; the national-versus-regional choice is open and the three national sources span about 7%.Caps the claimAdriaan
7. Institutional premises. Schools and health posts inside the service areas are not identified or counted; SDWS 24 carries separate defaults for them.Understates the claimMadAvance
8. The eight 2.2.1(d) records. Eight rehabilitations whose eligibility record is missing or answered No; the eligibility table gives each one’s state, and a point already excluded from the portfolio has nothing left to remove.Removes points if unresolvedMadAvance
9. Endur’O direct data access. Meter readings are visible only through an Endur’O dashboard we do not control, so they are a sighting, not evidence on file.Evidence chainAdriaan

How to read the ranking. The first three block issuance outright: each is a parameter a verifier must be able to check and currently cannot. Four to six cap the size of the claim rather than stopping it. Seven understates it — worth fixing because it works in our favour. Eight and nine are evidence-chain items that will be raised at validation whatever the numbers say.

Impact

Programme-level figures for donors and the website. Health impact is not yet computed — see note.

How these figures are built, and what is not in them yet

People served for hand pumps = Σ per pump WorldPop service-area estimate, capped at pump capacity — see “How the people-served figure is built” above. The MadAvance roof-count census is kept as a cross-check only. DALYs averted: no accepted number yet — propose WHO/IHME diarrhoeal-disease burden rates for Madagascar with the JMP "basic → safely managed" risk reduction applied to people served; agree the method with James before it goes in a donor report. Financial: no source connected (suggest a monthly extract: O&M cost per pump, carbon revenue, water-credit sales).

    Map count versus register count. The map draws all 745 hand pumps under active management; the population allocation covers 745 of them, and the build reruns the allocation whenever a pump joins or leaves (tools/rerun_wpop.py). One point’s coordinates are read from its register record rather than from the group export. Water point 742896839 has a complete register record, a GPS fix and three photographs, but its _managed_by is all rather than the MadAvance group, so every group-filtered export skips it — open action Bring water point 742896839 into the MadAvance register.

    Correction — DOp,y was described wrongly on this page. Earlier editions stated, or let the reader infer, that SDWS 27 days operational is indexed per water point, and that without current calendars each point is capped at 347 days. Both were wrong. In ERSDWS the parameter is days the project technology is operational for end-users in premises p in year y, and p is the premises type — the same p as SDWS 25 and SDWS 26 — entering Qpop,y = Σp HHp,y × HNp,y × QPWp × DOp,y. The calendars are the per-pump O&M record the parameter is built from, not the parameter itself. And the 347-day ceiling belongs to the evidence route, not to the calendars: the methodology permits values above 347 days only where an operation sensor is used, so under an O&M log the ceiling stands however complete the calendars are. The statements have been corrected wherever they appeared; this note stays so the change is visible rather than silent.

    Methodology of record. Every parameter reading in this report is checked against ERSDWS v1.0, the version the VPA is registered under — the Design Review assurance form names it throughout as the applied methodology. Both v1.0 and v2.0 are now held in Water Documents/Methodology of record/ with checksums and retrieval date. v2.0 enters into force approximately 7 October 2026 (§3.3.1, 90 days from publication on 9 July 2026); whether it applies to this VPA before renewal is with the Head of Carbon. The VPA-DD of record is not copied into the hub — it lives in the Carbon2 submission tree, and the hub points at it there, because two copies of a design document is how a verifier ends up reading the wrong one.

    SDWS 27 as registered. The VPA-DD applies 347 days for DOp,y, with the QA/QC condition that “values higher than 347 days may only be applied when option 1 is used” — option 1 being direct measurement by operation sensor — and the note that “operational sensors may be applied on a (90/10) sample basis to assess operational days in the Project scenario”. The sampling provision attaches to sensors, not to the calendars. The calendars are option 2, the operation and maintenance log, and they evidence the 347.
